In `checkIfIsAvailable`, when a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot falls inside the override window, the `dateOverrides.find(...)` callback returns `undefined` for that override, so the outer `if` is false and execution reaches `if (dateOverrideExist) return true;` (line 133-135). This returns early and completely skips the `busy.every(...)` loop below, meaning existing bookings, calendar busy times and buffers are ignored for any day that has a date override. Users can therefore be double-booked on date-override days. The override check should only decide whether the slot is inside the override window; the busy check must still run afterwards.

No test covers the main fix (date overrides of fixed hosts in round-robin) and the new timezone test is not sensitive to the organizer timezone

The PR's primary change is that fixed-host date overrides are honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events (via the new `dateOverrides`/`workingHours` arguments to `checkIfIsAvailable`), but no test creates a round-robin event with a fixed host that has a date override, so that code path is unverified. The added test only re-requests the same personal event with a different invitee timezone and asserts identical UTC slots; it does not exercise an organizer whose schedule timezone differs from the invitee's, and it does not cover a day that has both a date override and an existing booking (where the current implementation returns the slot as available).

Override offset depends on an optional `timeZone` that falls back to the server timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is used to compute the organizer offset, but `TimeRange.timeZone` is declared optional in `packages/types/schedule.d.ts`. If any caller of `getSlots` passes date overrides without `timeZone` (only the slots router was updated to attach it), `dayjs.tz(undefined)` resolves to the dayjs default/system timezone, producing a wrong organizer offset and silently shifted override slots instead of an error. Either make `timeZone` required for the overrides consumed here or explicitly fall back to the organizer timezone already passed into `getSlots`.

Timezone-shifted date override wraps around midnight and silently loses availability

The override start/end are converted to minutes-of-day with `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. When the invitee/organizer offset difference pushes the override across a day boundary (e.g. organizer 22:00-23:00 with a +8h invitee, or 02:00 with a -5h invitee), `hour()` wraps to the other day, so `startTime` can become greater than `endTime`. `buildSlots` then drops such a range via its `if (start >= end) continue` guard (or produces slots at completely wrong times), so the override silently yields no availability for invitees in far-away timezones.

Working-hours predicate marks a slot unavailable if ANY working-hour range does not contain it

The new check uses `workingHours.find(workingHour => ... if (start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime) return true)` and then treats a match as "slot is outside of working hours" -> unavailable. Because `find` succeeds as soon as one range does not contain the slot, any schedule with more than one availability range applicable to the same weekday (split days such as 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-18:00, or ranges split across UTC midnight by `getWorkingHours`) will cause every slot to be rejected, producing an empty schedule. The predicate must instead require that *no* range contains the slot (e.g. `!workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(day) && start >= wh.startTime && end <= wh.endTime)`).

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is the deterministic pipeline signature, so the state check gives no CSRF protection

The authorize redirect uses `state = pipeline.signature` and the callback only checks `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. The pipeline signature is deterministic and not user/session specific — the new tests hardcode the same value `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` for different users and organizations (`test_github_installed_on_another_org`, `test_github_user_mismatch`, `test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete`). An attacker can therefore construct a callback URL with a valid `state` plus their own `code`, and if a victim with an in-flight pipeline loads it, the attacker's GitHub identity gets bound into the victim's pipeline via `github_authenticated_user` — exactly the class of attack this PR is meant to prevent. The state should be a per-pipeline random nonce stored in pipeline state and compared on return.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError on integration.metadata["sender"] when metadata has no sender

`GitHubInstallation.dispatch` reaches `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` whenever an `Integration` row exists for the `installation_id` but no `OrganizationIntegration` rows exist. `metadata["sender"]` is only populated by `build_integration` when the pipeline/webhook state contains `sender` (see `build_integration`: `if state.get("sender")`), and integrations created through the normal pipeline do not have it — `tests/.../test_integration.py::test_basic_flow` asserts the saved metadata contains only access_token/expires_at/icon/domain_name/account_type. So for any integration whose OrganizationIntegration was hard-deleted (e.g. org deletion) or that was created without a sender, a re-install attempt raises `KeyError: 'sender'` and the user gets a 500 instead of the intended error page. Use `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and decide explicitly what to do when the sender is unknown.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing

false_positives.candidate:
Authenticated GitHub user is not verified when the Integration row does not yet exist

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, if `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the pipeline advances immediately (`return pipeline.next_step()`) without any comparison of `github_authenticated_user` against the account that installed the app. The sender information this check relies on is written by the asynchronous `installation` webhook, so whether the validation runs at all depends on webhook delivery timing: an attacker who knows a victim's `installation_id` and completes the redirect before the webhook is processed bypasses the new check entirely. The installation ownership should be verified against the authenticated user's own token (e.g. `GET /user/installations`) rather than relying on a pre-existing Integration row.

Unhandled exceptions from token exchange / get_user_info produce a 500 instead of the error page

`safe_urlopen(...)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are called without exception handling. `get_user_info` performs an HTTP request and raises `ApiError`/`ApiHostError` on non-2xx or network failures (e.g. revoked token, GitHub outage, rate limiting), and `safe_urlopen` raises on connection errors. Only the JSON/body parse is wrapped in `try/except`. The result is an unhandled 500 in the install popup rather than the intended `github-integration-failed.html` page, with no log line to diagnose it. Wrap both calls and fall back to `error(request, self.active_organization)` (plus a log).

gettext applied to a runtime variable breaks string extraction for the short error messages

`error()` wraps its `error_short` argument at call time with `_(error_short)`. Because the argument is a variable rather than a literal inside the `_()` call, `makemessages` cannot extract strings like "GitHub installation pending deletion." or "Github installed on another Sentry organization." anymore (previously they were literals inside `_()`), so these user-facing strings will silently stop being translated. Pass already-lazy/translated values from the call sites instead of translating the variable.

test_installation_not_found no longer exercises the 404 installation path

This test previously asserted `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."`, covering the `ApiError(404) -> IntegrationError` branch in `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration`. It now passes `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"`, a different value from the `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` signature used by every other test in this file, and asserts only the generic `b"Invalid installation request."`. The request therefore short-circuits in `OAuthLoginView` on the state mismatch and the 404 handling in `build_integration` is no longer covered by any test. Either restore the correct state so the flow reaches `build_integration`, or add a separate test for the invalid-state branch and keep a real installation-not-found test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued` default is evaluated once at import time

`queued: datetime = timezone.now()` is a dataclass field default, so `timezone.now()` is called exactly once when the module is imported. Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` value therefore carries the process/module import timestamp, not the time the assignment was actually queued. This makes the field useless (and actively misleading) for debugging or any future staleness/TTL logic built on it. Use `field(default_factory=timezone.now)` instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Datetime in to_dict() is passed as Celery task kwargs and is not round-tripped by from_dict()

`to_dict()` returns `asdict(self)`, which keeps `queued` as a `datetime`. That dict is handed to `sync_assignee_outbound.apply_async(kwargs={... 'assignment_source_dict': ...})` (src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py:141), so a raw `datetime` ends up in the broker payload. Depending on the configured serializer this either fails to encode (the task is never enqueued and assignee sync silently stops) or arrives as an ISO string, in which case `from_dict` happily constructs an `AssignmentSource` whose `queued` attribute is a `str` despite the declared `datetime` type. Serialize/deserialize the timestamp explicitly (e.g., `isoformat()` / `fromisoformat()`) so the dataclass invariants hold across the task boundary.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.

false_positives.candidate:
New `assignment_source` kwarg passed to sync_assignee_outbound without updating the abstract signature

The task now calls `installation.sync_assignee_outbound(external_issue, user, assign=assign, assignment_source=parsed_assignment_source)`, but the abstract declaration in `IssueSyncIntegration.sync_assignee_outbound` (src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:397) was not updated to accept `assignment_source`; it only tolerates it via `**kwargs`. Any current or future implementation (including third-party/provider installations) that defines `sync_assignee_outbound(self, external_issue, user, assign=True)` without `**kwargs` will raise `TypeError` at runtime, and the retry decorator will retry it 5 times before failing. Declare `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` on the abstract method so the contract is explicit.

No test that a non-matching assignment source still propagates outbound

The new test only covers the case where the assignment source integration matches the target integration (sync suppressed). There is no test asserting the complementary behaviour that this PR explicitly promises: when the `AssignmentSource` comes from a *different* integration, the outbound sync must still fire. Without it, a regression that over-suppresses sync (e.g., comparing the wrong id field in `should_sync`) would go undetected and silently break cross-integration issue sync.

`assignment_source` added to abstract sync_status_outbound but never passed or used

The abstract `sync_status_outbound` signature gains an `assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None` parameter, but no caller in this PR passes it and no concrete implementation consumes it. The signature now advertises cycle protection for status sync that does not exist; worse, subclasses still declare `(self, external_issue, is_resolved, project_id, **kwargs)`, so a caller following the abstract contract and passing the source positionally would bind it to an unrelated kwarg position. Either wire the parameter through the status-sync path or drop it from the abstract signature.

from_dict silently swallows malformed payloads, disabling cycle protection without any signal

`from_dict` returns `None` for any payload that doesn't exactly match the constructor (missing key, extra key, renamed field) and performs no type validation on `integration_id`. Because `sync_assignee_outbound` treats `None` as "no source", a malformed/renamed payload means the loop-prevention check in `should_sync` is skipped and the sync cycle this PR is meant to fix silently returns, with nothing logged or metered to indicate it happened. Add a log/metric on the failure path (and validate `integration_id` is an int) so this failure mode is observable.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler is now abstract and cannot be instantiated

`MetricAlertDetectorHandler` now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler` with only `pass`, but `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares four abstract members (`counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and the newly added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`) and inherits `abc.ABC`. Because none of them are implemented, `MetricAlertDetectorHandler(detector)` raises `TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class ...`. This is reached from `Detector.detector_handler` for any detector of type `metric_alert_fire`, so `process_detectors` will blow up at runtime instead of returning no results (previously the handler returned `[]` safely). Either implement the abstract hooks or keep the class non-registered/abstract until they exist.

true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Multi-group test asserts occurrence built with the wrong value

`test_state_results_multi_group` sends `group_2` with value 10 but builds the expected occurrence with `value=6`. The test only passes because `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` ignores the `value` argument, so the test cannot detect if the wrong value is forwarded from `evaluate_group_key_value` to `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Make the mock occurrence depend on `value` (e.g. put it in `evidence_data`) and pass the real value, so the plumbing of `value` and `new_status` is actually verified.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

false_positives.candidate:
Stale TODO comment about stateful detector

The comment `# TODO: This will be a stateful detector when we build that abstraction` sits directly above a class that now subclasses `StatefulDetectorHandler`, so it is misleading to future readers. It should be removed or replaced with the actual remaining work (implementing the required abstract hooks).

get_state_data raises KeyError when counter_names is empty

In `get_state_data`, `counter_updates` is only populated inside `if self.counter_names:`; otherwise it stays `{}`. The loop below then unconditionally does `counter_updates[gk]`, which raises `KeyError` for a handler that legitimately tracks no counters (an empty `counter_names` list is a valid implementation of the abstract property). Use `counter_updates.get(gk, {})` or initialize the dict for all group keys.

true_positives.golden_comment: The function modifies the config variable to include display values but then returns the original monitor.config instead of the modified version.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
get_monitor_environment_context discards the modified config copy

`get_monitor_environment_context` makes a copy of `monitor.config`, replaces `schedule_type` with its human-readable display value, but then returns `monitor_environment.monitor.config` (the original, unmodified dict) under the `"config"` key. The `config` local is never used, so the monitor context attached to the issue occurrence still carries the raw integer `schedule_type` instead of the display string. This defect is being carried into the new module unchanged; since the code is being relocated anyway it is a good time to return `config` instead of `monitor_environment.monitor.config`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The code fetches MonitorCheckIn objects by ID when the required data already exists in previous_checkins. This creates an unnecessary database query.

false_positives.candidate:
Public symbols removed from mark_failed without re-export shims

`mark_failed_threshold`, `create_issue_platform_occurrence`, `get_failure_reason`, `get_monitor_environment_context`, `HUMAN_FAILURE_STATUS_MAP`, `SINGULAR_HUMAN_FAILURE_MAP` and `SimpleCheckIn` were all module-level names in `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed` and are now gone (moved and partially renamed). Any other module or test that imports them from this path, or that patches e.g. `sentry.monitors.logic.mark_failed.create_issue_platform_occurrence` / `mark_failed_threshold` with `mock.patch`, will now fail at import/patch time (mock.patch raises AttributeError for a missing attribute). No test files are updated in this PR, so please verify (grep for these names across src/ and tests/) and either update call sites/patch targets or keep thin re-export aliases in `mark_failed.py`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

The test still relies on the flusher thread having produced the message before `step.join()` returns, so the intended synchronization is absent and the test remains timing-dependent/flaky. true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

`_ensure_processes_alive` only kills the old worker if `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)`. The processes here are created via `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn").Process`, which produces `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` objects. `SpawnProcess` derives from `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`, not from `multiprocessing.context.Process` (which is what the module-level `multiprocessing.Process` alias resolves to), so the isinstance check is always False and `kill()` is never invoked. The previous code called `self.process.kill()` unconditionally. Consequence: when a flusher is detected as hung (`cause == "hang"`) the old process keeps running while a replacement is started for the same shards, so two processes concurrently flush the same Redis shards and produce duplicate/fragmented segments to `buffered-segments`, and leaked processes accumulate on every restart. true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() aborts the shutdown loop, leaving the remaining processes unterminated

In `join()`, when the deadline has passed the loop `break`s out before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for the remaining entries of `self.processes`. With more than one flusher process, a timed-out join therefore terminates only the processes iterated before the deadline expired; the rest are left running and continue flushing segments while the consumer is shutting down/rebalancing. (Additionally, `remaining_time` is computed but never used, and the `terminate()` call itself is dead for spawn processes because of the same `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` problem.) Terminate every process unconditionally after the wait loop.

false_positives.candidate:
A new SpansBuffer (and its Redis clients) is created in the parent on every restart without releasing the old one

`_create_process_for_shards` constructs a fresh `SpansBuffer(shards)` and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting the previous instance. The parent process keeps using these buffers for `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()`, so each unhealthy-process restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process) leaves the previous buffer's Redis connections unclosed in the parent. Reuse the existing buffer for the process index, or close the old one before replacing it.

Class docstring claims one process per shard and documents a non-existent param

The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the number of processes is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))`, and the consumer CLI defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, so the normal configuration is a single process handling all shards. The docstring also still documents `:param topic:` which is not an argument, and does not document the new `max_processes` argument. This misleads operators about the default parallelism.

Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` left behind

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). Dead code that duplicates restart logic is a maintenance hazard — a future caller would restart a whole process group from a single shard id. Remove it.

New multi-process flusher test only asserts bookkeeping, never exercises flushing across shards

`test_flusher_processes_limit` creates 4 partitions with `flusher_processes=2` but never submits a message and never asserts that segments from all 4 shards are produced. It only checks `len(flusher.processes)`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and the total shard count. The behaviour this PR actually changes — several shards being flushed by one worker, and all shards being covered by the shard->process mapping — is untested. Consider submitting spans for each partition and asserting that one produced message per shard arrives, and that `process_to_shards_map` is a partition of `assigned_shards` (no duplicates/omissions).

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behaviour the implementation does not provide and is timing dependent

The test's docstring says errors should not block offset commits, yet it asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. `OrderedQueueWorker.run` catches the processing exception and still calls `complete_offset` in its `finally`, so offsets 100 and 101 become committable and the commit loop (which ticks every ~1s) will commit them. The test only passes because it breaks out of the wait loop after a 0.2s sleep, before the first commit tick — i.e. it is flaky and encodes the opposite of the real behaviour. Either assert that failed messages are committed (documenting the at-most-once semantics) or implement and test actual retry/DLQ handling.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
A single missing offset permanently blocks all commits for the partition

`get_committable_offsets()` walks offsets contiguously from `last_committed + 1` and `break`s on the first offset that is not present in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous as seen by a consumer (transactional/control records, compaction, or any message that never reaches `submit` because an upstream wrapper such as the DLQ/stale-message wrapper consumed it). If one offset in the sequence is never added, that partition can never advance its commit point: `all_offsets` grows without bound and the consumer group lag never decreases, causing full reprocessing of everything after the gap on restart. There needs to be a mechanism to advance past offsets that will never be seen (e.g. seed the committed position from the assignment and treat unknown offsets below the current max as done).

Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`commit_offsets` (passed as `commit_function`) is called from `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the arroyo `StreamProcessor` concurrently polls and commits on the main thread. The `Commit` callable given to `create_with_partitions` stages/commits offsets on the shared consumer state and is expected to be called from the processing (main) thread; calling it concurrently races with the processor's own offset staging/commit and with partition revocation (where it can raise `ConsumerError` for unassigned partitions, silently swallowed by the loop's `except Exception`). This can produce lost or incorrect offset commits. Offsets should be collected by the background workers and committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the main thread instead.

Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys hash into exactly all 3 queues (`len(queue_indices) == 3`). `get_queue_for_group` uses `hash()` on a `str`, which is salted per interpreter run (PYTHONHASHSEED), so there is a small but non-zero chance (~0.1%) that one bucket receives no key and the test fails for unrelated reasons. Assert something weaker (e.g. `len(queue_indices) > 1`) or use a deterministic hash function.

Generic exception handler in submit() drops messages and commits their offsets

`submit()` wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one `try/except Exception`; on any failure (including a failing `grouping_fn`, a `FilteredPayload` payload which trips the `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` in `decode_payload`, or `queue.ShutDown` from a shut-down pool) it logs and then marks the offset as both added and completed. The message is silently discarded and its offset is committed, so the data is lost with no DLQ and no visible failure other than a log line. Expected non-processable cases (filtered payloads, decode failures) should be handled explicitly, and unexpected enqueue failures should either raise (so arroyo can DLQ/stop) rather than ack the offset.

Per-worker queue-depth gauge is emitted with identical tags from all workers

Every `OrderedQueueWorker` emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` with only an `identifier` tag, so all N workers (20 by default) report the depth of their own queue under the same metric series. The values overwrite each other and the resulting gauge is meaningless for diagnosing a backed-up individual queue — which is the main failure mode this design is meant to surface. Add a `worker_id`/queue index tag or emit the max/aggregate from one place.

Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close and then reused after rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, but the per-assignment strategy's `close()`/`terminate()`/`join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the worker threads. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on every partition revocation (rebalance), and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again for the new assignment. On that second call `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes, so a strategy is built around a pool whose worker threads are dead and whose queues are shut down: every `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` swallows in its generic `except Exception` handler and then marks the offset as completed. The consumer will therefore silently drop all messages while still committing their offsets after any rebalance. The pool must be created per assignment (or re-created in `create_with_partitions`) rather than shared across strategy lifetimes.

Unbounded queues mean no backpressure, contradicting the documented guarantee

Each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `arroyo.processing.strategies.abstract.MessageRejected`. As a result the strategy accepts messages from the Kafka consumer as fast as they arrive regardless of worker progress: work items (which also retain the full `Message`/`KafkaPayload`) and their tracked offsets accumulate in memory without bound when a group's processing is slow, which is exactly the scenario this PR is meant to address. This also contradicts the class docstring ("Natural backpressure when queues fill up"). A bounded queue plus `MessageRejected` on `queue.Full` is needed for arroyo to actually throttle consumption.

Worker transaction name hardcodes the "monitors" prefix

The sentry transaction created per work item is named `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this strategy is generic to remote subscriptions and is being enabled for the uptime consumer. Transactions for uptime results will be grouped under a `monitors.` namespace, making performance data misleading/hard to find.

close() stops the commit thread before draining queues, losing committable offsets

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, and only then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which drains the remaining queued items (`shutdown(immediate=False)` lets queued work finish). Any item processed during that drain completes its offset after the only thread that commits offsets has already exited, so those offsets are never committed. On restart/rebalance all of that work is reprocessed. Additionally `join(timeout)` ignores the supplied timeout and just calls `close()`, so arroyo's shutdown deadline is not honoured. The order should be: stop accepting work, drain the queues, perform a final `get_committable_offsets()` + commit, then stop the commit thread.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key built by naive concatenation can collide between distinct resources

`userPermDenialCacheKey` joins `action`, `name` and `parent` with single underscores without escaping. Since Grafana UIDs may contain underscores, distinct requests map to the same key: e.g. name=`a_b`/parent=`c` and name=`a`/parent=`b_c` both produce `...perm_<uid>_<action>_a_b_c`. A cached deny for one resource therefore denies access to a different resource for up to the TTL (and, less harmfully, the key shares the `".perm_"` prefix space with `userPermCacheKey`, so a colliding key makes the permission cache entry undecodable). Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions, or hash the components; also note the key omits group/resource and relies solely on the derived action string.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache can lock in a deny caused by a stale folder tree

`Check` now persists a negative result in `permDenialCache` for 30s whenever `checkPermission` returns false. The fallback added above only re-reads *permissions* from the DB; the folder hierarchy used by `checkInheritedPermissions` is still served from `folderCache` (also 30s TTL, see `buildFolderTree`). So for the exact case this PR targets – a resource that was just created in a folder the user only has inherited access to, or a brand-new folder – the folder tree lookup misses, the check is denied even after the fresh DB permission read, and that deny is then cached for the full TTL. The user is blocked for up to 30s even though a re-read of folders would have allowed access. Either skip caching the denial when the decision depended on the folder tree, or invalidate/refresh the folder tree on the fallback path.

Every non-cached denial triggers a full permission re-query and an unbounded cache entry

The cache read was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` now falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (DB query for basic role, teams and permissions) whenever the cached scope map does not grant the requested resource. Combined with a denial cache keyed by `(namespace, user, action, name, parentFolder)`, any sequence of checks over distinct resource names the user cannot access produces one DB permission query per distinct name, and one new cache entry per distinct name. For bulk authorization (e.g. checking many dashboards during a search) or for a caller passing arbitrary names, this is a significant DB-load amplification versus the previous behaviour (single cached scope map), and the local cache grows without bound until TTL expiry. Consider rate-limiting the re-query (e.g. a short "recently refreshed" marker per user+action) instead of re-querying on every miss.

permissionCacheUsage metric records a miss when the cache was actually hit

When `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeds but the cached scope map does not grant access, control falls through to line 137 and increments `permissionCacheUsage` with label `"false"` (miss), even though the permission cache was hit. Because the per-function metric increments were removed from `getUserPermissions`, this is now the only accounting point, so cache hit-rate dashboards will systematically under-report hits for denied checks and make the new caching behaviour impossible to evaluate.

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, where `isFederated` is hardcoded to `false` (line 245, with only a TODO). The menu now computes `canPause`/`canDelete` from the Prometheus-rule abilities as well (so that the list view works without ruler requests), but the render conditions are still `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123) and `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165). The test therefore encodes incorrect expectations and gives false confidence. It also does not cover the regression the PR fixes: that the interpolated `step` is used when computing the partitions (e.g. asserting the number/size of sub-requests changes when `step: '$step'` resolves to a large interval).
