TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs, making log assertions useless

`TestLogger.FromContext` returns a brand new `TestLogger` instead of `f` (or a logger that writes back into `f`'s `Logs` fields). After this PR `LoggerMiddleware.logRequest` logs via `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)`, so any test that injects a `TestLogger` into `NewLoggerMiddleware` and then asserts on `InfoLogs.Calls`/`Message`/`Ctx` will always see zero calls, even though the code logged. This silently removes the ability to unit-test the plugin request logging (and any other code path that uses `FromContext`). It should return the same instance (or a child that records into the parent's slices).

false_positives.candidate:
Adding FromContext to the Logger interface breaks all existing implementors

`FromContext(ctx context.Context) Logger` is added to the `plugins/log.Logger` interface. Every type implementing this interface must now provide the method; only `grafanaInfraLogWrapper` and `TestLogger` are updated in this PR. Any other implementation in the repository (fakes/mocks in other packages, embedded wrappers) will fail to compile, and out-of-tree implementations break. Confirm there are no other implementors, or provide an embeddable base/no-op implementation.

LoggerMiddleware silently loses pluginId/endpoint/dsName/uname unless ContextualLoggerMiddleware runs before it

The log parameters `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID` were removed from `logRequest` and are now expected to come from the contextual logger installed by the new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware`. This creates an undocumented ordering dependency: if `NewLoggerMiddleware` is used without `NewContextualLoggerMiddleware`, or the latter is registered after it in the chain (e.g. other call sites building their own middleware list, Enterprise code, or tests), the "Plugin Request Completed" egress log silently degrades to status/duration only, breaking log-based dashboards/alerts on these fields. At minimum document the requirement on both middlewares (the old `InstrumentationMiddleware` carried a "should live at the top of the middleware stack" comment, which was dropped), and ideally add a test asserting the egress log contains the plugin fields.

No test coverage for the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware

The PR extracts contextual-logging behaviour into a new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` and makes `LoggerMiddleware` depend on it, but no test is added for either. Nothing verifies that `endpoint`, `pluginId`, `dsName`, `dsUID` and `uname` end up in the context (and thus in the egress log line), so a future regression in this middleware or in middleware ordering would go unnoticed. Also, the renamed test still declares `func TestInstrumentationMiddleware`, which no longer matches the `MetricsMiddleware` name it exercises.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Check-then-insert on device count is racy and can exceed the configured limit

`CreateOrUpdateDevice` performs `CountDevices` and then, in a separate session, an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. Concurrent anonymous requests for new device IDs can all read a count below `deviceLimit` and then all insert, so the stored device count can exceed the configured limit by the number of concurrent requests. Since the limit is a licensing/abuse control, this is an enforcement hole. Consider doing the count and insert inside one transaction, or enforcing the limit with a conditional INSERT (e.g. `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`) so the check and write are atomic.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
rowsAffected == 0 wrongly reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached for existing devices on MySQL

`updateDevice` maps `rowsAffected == 0` to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. On MySQL, `RowsAffected()` reports *changed* rows, not matched rows (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set), so an UPDATE that matches an already-tracked device but writes identical column values (same client_ip/user_agent and an `updated_at` that truncates to the same second — MySQL DATETIME has second precision here) returns 0. In that case an existing, already-counted device is denied access with "device limit reached" even though it is within the limit. Additionally, this error value conflates two distinct conditions ("device not found/expired" vs "limit reached"), which makes the surfaced error misleading; the device-not-found case should be distinguished or detected via a SELECT/matched-rows check.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the store call, so the device limit is bypassed after the first rejection

In `tagDeviceUI` the cache entry is written (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is invoked. With the new limit logic, the first request from an over-limit device returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and is denied, but the cache key is already set, so every subsequent request from that same device for the cache TTL (29 min) short-circuits with `return nil` and is authenticated without ever consulting the limit. The result is that the configured `device_limit` is enforced only on the very first request per device per cache window, i.e. effectively not enforced, and users see a confusing "fails once then works" behaviour. The cache should only be populated after a successful store call (or the failed key removed on error).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips to every anonymous request

`TagDevice` was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own timeout; it is now called synchronously inside `Authenticate`. Every anonymous request whose device ID is not in the 29-minute local cache now blocks on a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device` (when `device_limit > 0`) plus an INSERT/UPDATE before authentication completes. For instances with high anonymous traffic and many distinct device IDs this adds DB load and request latency on the hot login path, and a slow/locked DB now stalls (rather than merely fails to record) anonymous requests. If synchronous behaviour is required only to enforce the limit, consider only doing the blocking path when a limit is configured, and/or caching the device count.

ErrDeviceLimitReached is a plain error, so clients get an opaque 500 instead of an actionable status

`ErrDeviceLimitReached` is created with `fmt.Errorf`, and `client.go` returns it directly from `Authenticate`. Because it carries no `errutil` status/public message, the authn broker will surface it as a generic internal error (HTTP 500 with no meaningful message) to the browser, so an operator-configured device limit looks like a server failure to the end user and is hard to diagnose from the response. Define it with `errutil` (e.g. a 429/403-style status with a public message) so the limit rejection is reported as an intentional, documented condition.

New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not added to defaults.ini/sample.ini or documented

`cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` introduces a new user-facing configuration key `[auth.anonymous] device_limit`, but the PR does not add it to `conf/defaults.ini`/`conf/sample.ini` nor to the configuration docs. Without the defaults.ini entry the option is undiscoverable (and the documented-config consistency checks Grafana runs over defaults.ini/docs will flag it), and operators have no documentation of the behaviour when the limit is hit (new devices are rejected, existing devices continue to work).

No test for the main intended path: updating an already-tracked device while at the limit

`TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device ID is rejected once the limit is reached. The core behaviour of the feature — that an already-stored device keeps working (its client_ip/user_agent/updated_at are updated) when the count is at or above `deviceLimit` — is untested, as is the expiry window in `updateDevice` (a device older than `anonymousDeviceExpiration` should not be revived). These are exactly the paths where the `rowsAffected == 0` heuristic can misfire, so they should be covered.

Provider signature change (AnonStore -> db.DB) requires DI wiring updates not included in this PR

`ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer accepts an `anonstore.AnonStore` and instead takes `db.DB`, constructing the store internally, while `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a second `deviceLimit int64` parameter. No changes to the wire provider sets (`pkg/server/wire.go` and the enterprise equivalents) are included. If `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` / `wire.Bind(new(anonstore.AnonStore), ...)` are still listed there, wire generation will fail (no provider for `int64`, and/or an unused provider), breaking the build; conversely any other consumer that relied on injecting an `AnonStore` now loses it. The DI configuration needs to be updated in the same change.

anonymousDeviceLimit initialised to undefined narrows its type to `undefined`

`anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` with no type annotation makes the class property's inferred type `undefined`, so any frontend code that tries to use it numerically (e.g. `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0`) will be a type error even though the backend always sends a number. Note also that the Go DTO field has no `omitempty`, so the value is `0` (not absent) when the limit is disabled; annotate as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined` (or `number`) and make the frontend contract explicit about 0 meaning "no limit".

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping every ID of every batch

Six new `r.log.Error(...)` calls were added in `CleanAnnotations` (lines 534, 537, 554, 557) and `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` (lines 576, 579). These are informational/debug messages ("Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned tags", ...) emitted at ERROR level on every batch iteration of a job that runs continuously, and they include the full `ids` slice (up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` entries, 32767 in the new test) plus a nil `err`. Consequences: operators' error logs/alerting will fire on normal cleanup activity, and log volume/allocation becomes huge on large installations. These should be removed or downgraded to Debug without the full ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup job ticker reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute

`ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` changes the global cleanup service interval from 10 minutes to 1 minute. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and looks like leftover local debugging. It makes every cleanup job (tmp file scan, expired snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs, query history row-limit enforcement) run 10x more often, multiplying DB and filesystem load on all Grafana instances; note also that `clean()` has a 9-minute timeout, so a long-running sweep is immediately followed by another. This change should be reverted unless intentional and documented.

false_positives.candidate:
O(n^2) string building for SQLite inline ID list

In `deleteByIDs`, the SQLite branch builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop. Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so for a batch of ~32k IDs (the size exercised by the new test) this performs ~32k allocations and copies of an ever-growing ~200KB string, i.e. gigabytes of memcpy per batch, repeated for every batch of the cleanup loop. Use a `strings.Builder` (or `strconv.AppendInt` into a byte slice, as done elsewhere in this file) instead.

Placeholder-limit workaround only covers SQLite; large batch sizes can fail on MySQL/Postgres

`deleteByIDs` only avoids bind parameters when `GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999`. For MySQL and Postgres the code always emits one `?` per ID, but both have a hard limit of 65535 bind parameters per statement. An operator who sets `annotation_cleanup_job_batch_size` above 65535 will get a hard driver error on every cleanup cycle instead of a degraded-but-working job. Either cap the number of IDs per DELETE statement (chunking) regardless of dialect, or gate on `len(ids)` against a per-dialect limit.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete puts the base logger in the context instead of the enriched one

`Delete` builds `log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)` but then does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`. Downstream code that retrieves the logger via `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the name/kind/method values, making delete-path logs from the storage and legacy layers unattributable. Should be `klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` as in the other methods.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Object name passed as the `kind` metric label in Delete causes unbounded label cardinality

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Because `name` is a per-object identifier, each deleted resource creates a new Prometheus time series on the storage duration histogram, leading to unbounded cardinality and potential memory blow-up in both Grafana and the scraping Prometheus. It also makes the metric unusable for comparison with the other label values. Use `options.Kind`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive from the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine that does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the *request* context. The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which in practice happens before or right after the goroutine starts. The derived context is therefore already (or immediately) cancelled, so the legacy store call will typically fail with `context canceled` and the legacy database will never be updated. Since mode 3's whole purpose is to keep legacy storage in sync as a safety net, this silently defeats the feature (errors are only recorded in a duration metric, never logged). Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving user/identity values) as the parent before applying the timeout.

Create records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure

In `Create`, when `d.Storage.Create` fails the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. This attributes a unified-storage failure/latency to the legacy backend metric, so the legacy error rate/latency dashboards will show failures that never happened in legacy, and unified-storage create failures are invisible in the storage metric. It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records a storage duration instead of a legacy duration

Inside the background goroutine of `DeleteCollection`, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` with `startLegacy`. This reports legacy latency/errors under the unified-storage metric, double counting storage observations for delete-collection and leaving legacy delete-collection completely unmeasured. Should be `recordLegacyDuration`.

Fire-and-forget goroutines have no panic recovery and no error logging

Each write path launches a bare `go func()` that calls into the legacy store. If the legacy implementation panics (e.g. nil map, nil pointer in a legacy service), the panic is not recovered inside the goroutine and the whole apiserver process crashes – unlike the synchronous path, where the apiserver's handler-level recovery would convert it to a 500. The goroutines also discard the legacy error entirely (only `err != nil` is folded into a histogram label), so operators have no way to find out which objects failed to mirror. Add `defer recover()` with logging and log the legacy error with the object name/kind.

Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object already persisted in unified storage

The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` with `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so that legacy storage persisted exactly the object that unified storage had stored. Now the original `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update` from a goroutine. `objInfo.UpdatedObject` will be re-evaluated against legacy's own `old` object, which has a different resourceVersion than unified storage, so for PUT (which carries a resourceVersion) legacy updates can fail with a conflict, and for PATCH/apply the transformers run a second time against a different base producing a different result. The net effect is silent divergence between unified and legacy data – the opposite of what mode 3's legacy mirror is for. Additionally `objInfo`/`obj` are request-scoped values that are now read concurrently after the handler has returned, which is not guaranteed to be safe.

Mode 3 integration tests assert legacy state immediately after k8s writes, which is now asynchronous

The three new mode-3 sub-tests (file line 132, unified line 191, etcd line 287) run `doPlaylistTests`, which after creating playlists through the k8s client immediately queries the legacy endpoint `/api/playlists` and requires the same UIDs (line 523-531), and after each k8s update calls `getFromBothAPIs` comparing legacy DTO fields (line 547). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a detached goroutine with no synchronization, so these assertions race against the background write and the tests will be flaky – and given the cancelled-context problem in the goroutine they are likely to fail deterministically. The tests need to poll/retry the legacy endpoint, or mode 3 must flush legacy writes before responding.

NotFound from unified storage now aborts the legacy delete, leaving orphan legacy rows

The previous mode 3 `Delete` explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. The new code returns early on any storage error, so an object that exists only in legacy (e.g. created before the migration, or whose earlier async legacy mirror failed) can never be deleted from legacy via the API. These orphan rows will resurface if the deployment is ever moved back to a mode that reads from legacy (modes 0–2).

Unit tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy write

All mode-3 write tests (`Create`, `Delete`, `Update`, `DeleteCollection`) assert only on the value returned from unified storage and return immediately; nothing calls `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` or waits for the goroutine that performs the legacy write. The central new behaviour of mode 3 – that legacy is also written – is therefore completely untested (the cancelled-context bug above would not be caught). Worse, the goroutine may invoke the shared `mock.Mock` after the sub-test has finished; if the arguments don't match a registered expectation testify panics from that goroutine and takes down the whole test binary. Add a synchronization point (e.g. a channel closed from the mock's Run function) and assert the legacy call happened with the expected arguments.

Update records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure

In `Update`, the error branch calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the failure came from `d.Storage.Update`. Same consequence as in `Create`: legacy metrics get polluted with unified-storage failures and storage failures are not counted. Should be `recordStorageDuration`.

go.work.sum contains a duplicated entry and unrelated dependency churn

The added block duplicates the line `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:...` that already exists a few lines above, and inserts entries out of sorted order (grafana-azure-sdk-go after grafana/pkg/apimachinery). This indicates the file was hand-edited rather than regenerated with `go work sync`/`go mod tidy`; it is also unrelated to the dual-writer change and will churn/conflict with other PRs. Regenerate the file or drop these hunks from this PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Double-checked locking is missing the second check inside the write lock

After the fast path with the read lock fails, the function takes the write lock but never re-reads `entryPointAssetsCache`. If N goroutines reach this point concurrently at startup (the common case, since the cache is cold while the first requests arrive), each one in turn will acquire the write lock and redo the full manifest load (file read + JSON decode, or an HTTP fetch to the CDN) and overwrite the cache, even though the first one already populated it. Re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `Lock()` removes this thundering-herd work.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
A failed load overwrites a previously valid cache with nil

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, including when `readWebAssetsFromFile`/`readWebAssetsFromCDN` returned an error and `result == nil`. In that case a previously successfully cached value is destroyed and the function returns `nil, err`, so every subsequent call must retry the load and callers that don't check the error can get a nil pointer. The assignment should only happen when `err == nil && result != nil`.

false_positives.candidate:
Blocking I/O performed while holding the write lock

The file read and the (currently dead, but still reachable) CDN HTTP request at lines 54-67 are executed while the exclusive `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` is held, so all other callers of `GetWebAssets` — including those that would be served from cache in dev mode or during cache refreshes — block on network/disk latency. Loading outside the lock and only taking the write lock to publish the result would avoid serializing request handling on I/O.

No test covering the concurrent access being fixed

The PR fixes a data race on the `entryPointAssetsCache` global but adds no test. A simple test that calls `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines (which fails under `-race` before the fix) would prevent the race from being reintroduced, e.g. by a future refactor that drops the mutex.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions() is dead, self-contradictory logic

`enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` (note the inverted sense: `enabled` is true when the flag is *off*) and then returns `false` from both branches, so the feature-flag lookup has no effect at all. The intent (always disable SQL expressions) is achieved only by accident of the final `return false`. This is a trap for the next maintainer: anyone re-enabling the feature by deleting the `if` block would end up enabling SQL expressions exactly when the toggle is disabled, and vice versa. It should be a plain unconditional disable (or a correctly-oriented flag check) with a comment referencing CVE-2024-9264.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy SQL command path now fails with an opaque 'error reading SQL command'

`NewSQLCommand` still calls `sql.TablesList`, which now unconditionally fails because `DB.RunCommands` returns `errors.New("not implemented")`. The caller converts this into `errutil.BadRequest("sql-invalid-sql")` with public message "error reading SQL command", so any existing panel or alert rule using a SQL expression (through `UnmarshalSQLCommand`, the non-reader path) breaks with a message suggesting the user's SQL is malformed rather than that the feature has been disabled. It also logs the full raw SQL at Warn level on every such request. Prefer short-circuiting with an explicit "SQL expressions are disabled" error.

false_positives.candidate:
DB.TablesList stub is unused dead code

`DB.TablesList` is never called: `pkg/expr/sql/parser.go` uses the package-level `TablesList` function, which goes through `DB.RunCommands`. Keeping an unused method on the stub type adds confusion about which entry point actually gates SQL execution; either remove it or make the package-level function delegate to it.

Error message does not explain that the feature was intentionally removed

Returning `fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented")` for `QueryTypeSQL` is misleading for operators who have explicitly enabled the still-registered `sqlExpressions` feature toggle: it reads like a missing implementation rather than a deliberate security-driven disable. Users will have no indication why their previously working queries fail. Mention that SQL expressions are disabled in this build/version (and consider removing or marking the feature toggle as non-functional so the documented toggle doesn't advertise a capability that no longer exists).

No regression test asserting SQL expressions are rejected

This change is a security fix (CVE-2024-9264) whose entire effect is that `QueryTypeSQL` queries must be rejected and that `sql.DB` never executes anything. There is no test covering `ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery` with `type: sql` returning an error (with the feature toggle both on and off), nor one covering `NewSQLCommand`/`sql.TablesList` failing. Without such a test, a future refactor of `enableSqlExpressions` or re-introduction of a real `DB` implementation can silently reopen the RCE/LFI path.

NoData result is immediately overwritten by TableData

In `Execute`, when `frame.Rows() == 0` the code sets `rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.NoData{Frame: frame}}` but the following statement unconditionally reassigns `rsp.Values = mathexp.Values{mathexp.TableData{Frame: frame}}`, so the NoData branch can never take effect and empty results are always reported as an empty table. The second assignment needs to be in an `else` branch. (Pre-existing, but this file is being touched and the dead branch will mislead future readers.)

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate index builds for the same key

BuildIndex previously held `b.cacheMu` for the whole function, which serialized builds and guaranteed that only one index per NamespacedResource was ever constructed. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. Nothing prevents two goroutines from calling BuildIndex for the same key concurrently (e.g. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does an unsynchronized GetIndex-then-build, and it is reachable from both the watch-event handler and concurrent Search calls). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, so the second call fails with a 'path already exists' error and the request errors out; (2) duplicated full index builds waste CPU/IO; (3) the loser's bleve index is overwritten in the cache and never closed, leaking file handles/memory. If the goal is finer-grained locking, a per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed rather than no mutual exclusion at all.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map under `b.cacheMu` from arbitrary goroutines (index builds triggered by watch events or search requests). Concurrent map read and map write is a fatal, unrecoverable Go runtime error ('concurrent map read and map write') that crashes the process. Previously this was partially masked because BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole duration; with the finer locking, writes happen far more often and at unpredictable times. TotalDocs should take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`.

false_positives.candidate:
Index build now runs synchronously in the constructor with an uncancellable, unbounded context

`s.Init(ctx)` is invoked from `NewResourceServer` with a `context.Background()`-derived context that has no deadline, and it performs the full search index build (`searchSupport.init`, which lists every resource of every namespace). Constructing the resource server therefore blocks Grafana/storage-server startup for as long as indexing takes, with no timeout and no way for the caller to cancel; a slow or unresponsive database makes startup hang indefinitely rather than failing or degrading. Consider a bounded context or kicking the index build off asynchronously while keeping the lifecycle/backend init synchronous.

Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the server context and background goroutines

`NewResourceServer` creates `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` and stores `cancel` on the server. When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, the function returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during Init — the storage backend's watch poller started by `searchSupport.init` via `WatchWriteEvents`, and the broadcaster/watcher if `initWatcher` partially succeeded — keeps running against a context that is never cancelled, leaking goroutines, DB connections and the context itself for the lifetime of the process. Call `cancel()` (or `s.Stop`) on the error path.

Removing per-request Init() checks means requests are still served after Stop()

`Stop` communicates shutdown by setting `s.initErr = "service is stopping"` / `"service is stopped"`, and the only thing that ever read `initErr` on the request path were the `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil` guards that this PR deleted from Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/History/Origin/IsHealthy/PutBlob/GetBlob. After this change, requests arriving after `Stop()` no longer fail fast; they fall through to a backend whose context has been cancelled, producing confusing 'context canceled' errors (or, for blob/diagnostics paths, operating on torn-down state) instead of the intended shutdown error. Either keep a cheap state check at the entry of the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` shutdown signalling in `Stop`.

Storage-server integration test now skipped for postgres, leaving only mysql coverage

With sqlite3 already skipped, adding an unconditional skip for postgres means `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` only ever runs against mysql in CI. Given this PR changes resource-server startup to initialize unified storage (including index building) inside `NewResourceServer`, the postgres startup path is exactly what this test would have covered. The TODO has no tracking issue; at minimum reference one so the coverage gap is not forgotten.

errgroup goroutines share the outer `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables (data race, lost errors)

Inside `group.Go(...)` the code does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigning to the `err` declared in the enclosing function, and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed`. With `initWorkers > 1` these are concurrent unsynchronized writes: a genuine data race (will be flagged by `-race`) and, worse, one goroutine's error can be clobbered by another goroutine before `group.Wait()` returns, and `err = group.Wait()` can be overwritten by a still-running assignment. Since this function now runs at server construction and its error aborts startup, misreporting matters. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic counter.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup registers removal of a non-existent IDP alias ("alias") instead of the created one

`getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove)` uses the literal string "alias" rather than the alias actually created (`idp-alias-<i>`, and `idp-alias-20` on line 425). Consequently (a) the cleanup call targets a provider that never exists, so it will fail/throw at teardown, and (b) the realm-level providers created by this test (`idp-alias-0`..`idp-alias-9`, which are not linked to an organization and therefore not removed together with the organizations) are left behind in the shared test realm. Any other test in the class that counts identity providers or login-eligible providers can then fail depending on JUnit method ordering. The alias must be captured in a local final variable and used in the cleanup lambda.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation on update is decided from the organization-aware wrapper, so it depends on transient organization state

`update()` passes `idpById` (obtained from `getById()`, which returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`) into `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the organization provider for the realm) is disabled, even though the stored IDP row is enabled. As a result `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` can evaluate to `false` for an IDP that *is* present in the cached login ID sets (the DB query behind `getForLogin` only filters on the IDP's own `enabled` flag, not on the organization state). In that situation an update that really removes the IDP from the login set (e.g. setting `hideOnLogin=true` or clearing `kc.org.broker.public`) takes the `!test(original) && !test(updated)` early return and does *not* invalidate `*.idp.login.*`. Because enabling/disabling an organization (a group attribute change) also does not invalidate those keys, after the organization is re-enabled `getForLogin` keeps returning the now hidden/non-public provider - `getForLogin` never re-applies the login predicate to the re-resolved models, and callers only re-check `isEnabled()`. Note the inconsistency with `remove()`, which correctly uses the unwrapped `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`; `update()` should likewise use the raw stored model (or compare only the IDP's own fields).

New invalidation paths in create()/remove() are only tested for the negative case

The test only removes `idp-alias-1` (a disabled provider, i.e. not login-eligible) and only creates `idp-alias-20` with `hideOnLogin=true`, so both assertions verify that the login caches are *not* invalidated. The newly added `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(model)` in `create()` and `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` in `remove()` are therefore never exercised in their positive branch: a regression that drops either call (leaving the login caches stale after adding or deleting a login-eligible broker) would not be caught. Add a case that creates an enabled, non-hidden provider and one that removes a login-eligible provider, and assert the `*.idp.login.*` entries disappear.

Search key includes organizationId even for REALM_ONLY, and per-organization entries accumulate without bound

The search key is always derived from `organizationId`, but for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the delegate ignores `organizationId` entirely (it forces `ORGANIZATION_ID=null`). Any caller invoking `getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, someOrgId)` therefore creates a distinct search key for a logically identical result, and each new key triggers `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` plus a full re-query before being merged back. For `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL`, one cached `IdentityProviderListQuery` per realm accumulates one entry per organization id ever queried, with no bound or pruning, so memory grows with the number of organizations that are used for login. Consider using an empty search key for REALM_ONLY and bounding/keying per-organization results separately.

getForLogin now returns providers in non-deterministic order

The cached implementation collects internal ids into a `HashSet` and returns `new HashSet<>(...).stream()`, so the order of the returned providers is unspecified and can differ between calls/JVMs. Before this change the stream order followed the underlying query order (realm-level providers first, then organization providers, in the order produced by JPA). Callers that rely on a stable order or that take `findFirst()` on the result will now behave unpredictably; the login page happens to re-sort, but the SPI contract change affects every other consumer. Either preserve ordering (e.g. `LinkedHashSet`/list) or document that the order is undefined.

getLoginPredicate dereferences getConfig() which may be null

The new predicate does `Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))` whenever `idp.getOrganizationId() != null`. `IdentityProviderModel.getConfig()` is not guaranteed to be non-null (it can be set to `null` via `setConfig`, e.g. when a representation without a config is converted), so this can throw a `NullPointerException` from `create()`/`update()` in the Infinispan provider, which now calls the predicate on the caller-supplied model. Use a null-safe access (e.g. `idp.getConfig() != null && Boolean.parseBoolean(...)`) or `getConfig().getOrDefault` on a guaranteed map.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the default keystore's JDK provider

`getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, i.e. typically `SUN`, not a BouncyCastle provider. `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER` is derived from this provider's name and is used elsewhere as the explicit provider argument for `Signature.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER)`, `KeyFactory.getInstance(alg, PROVIDER)` etc. If any code reached with this crypto provider active uses `BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER`, it will request algorithms from a provider that does not implement them and fail with `NoSuchAlgorithmException`. Returning `null` (as `WildFlyElytronProvider` does) or throwing `UnsupportedOperationException` would make the unsupported nature explicit.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead encoder calls in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 create two `ASN1Encoder` instances, write `rBigInteger`/`sBigInteger` into them and discard the results; the actual DER sequence is built from freshly created encoders on lines 117-121. These two statements have no effect and only allocate; they should be removed to avoid suggesting the encoders are stateful/shared.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Indefinite-length encoding (-1) leads to NegativeArraySizeException instead of IOException

`readLength()` returns `-1` for the indefinite-length form (0x80), but callers do not handle it: `readInteger()` passes it directly to `read(length)`, which does `new byte[-1]` and throws an unchecked `NegativeArraySizeException`. Since this decoder parses attacker-controlled DER signature bytes, malformed input escapes as an unchecked exception rather than the declared `IOException` (and in `readSequence()` an indefinite length silently yields an empty list). DER does not allow indefinite lengths at all here, so `readLength()` should reject 0x80 with an `IOException`, or every caller must check for `-1`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`order()` added as abstract method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

`int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface without a `default` implementation. `CryptoProvider` is an SPI loaded via `ServiceLoader`, so any implementation outside this repository (adapters, downstream/3rd-party crypto providers, test doubles) will fail to compile and will throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` sorts providers. Giving the method a sensible `default` (e.g. `return 100;` or `0`) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still allowing providers to override the preference.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic string passed as format to logger.debugf

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a dynamically built message as the format string of a formatting logger method (with no arguments). Any `%` character appearing in a provider class name would cause an `UnknownFormatConversionException`/`MissingFormatArgumentException` from the logging call. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` or `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` instead.

ECDSA conversion test uses one default curve and never verifies the produced DER

The key pair is generated once with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` default parameters (P-256), so the ES384 and ES512 cases are exercised with 32-byte r/s values zero-padded to 48/66 bytes; the real cases (secp384r1/secp521r1 signatures, including the 521-bit odd byte length that is the usual source of off-by-one bugs) are never covered. In addition the test only asserts a round-trip of the new implementation against itself (`rsConcat` vs `rsConcat2`), so a systematic encoding error would pass. The test should generate a key per curve (`ECGenParameterSpec` secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the DER output with `Signature.verify()` (and/or compare with the BouncyCastle-based provider output).

Equal-order providers are now silently resolved instead of failing fast (FIPS vs non-FIPS)

The previous code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found, which protected against a misconfigured classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used unconditionally. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return `order() == 200`, so if e.g. both the default (non-FIPS BouncyCastle) and the FIPS provider jars end up on the classpath, the selection depends on undefined `ServiceLoader` iteration order and the server may silently start with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider in a deployment that must be FIPS-compliant, with only a debug-level log line. Either keep failing on an order tie, or give the server-side providers distinct orders and log at WARN when multiple providers of the same order are present.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER does not validate the input signature length

`System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)` / `System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len)` assume `signature.length == signLength`. For an attacker-supplied token whose signature part is shorter (or where the wrong algorithm length is used), this throws an unchecked `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` out of a method declared to throw `IOException`, so callers doing signature verification will see an unexpected runtime failure instead of a clean "invalid signature" error. The BouncyCastle-based implementations validate the length and throw `IOException`; the same check should be added here.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission returns the resource-type resource name and misses per-client resources

`getClientsWithPermission` iterates `resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients", ...)` and collects `resource.getName()`. Two problems: (1) the "all clients" resource created in `AdminPermissionsSchema.init()` has both name and type equal to `Clients`, so when an all-clients permission is granted the literal string `"Clients"` is added to the returned set and is then treated by callers as a client id; (2) per-client resources created by `AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource()` are created without a type (`setType` is never called), so `findByType` never returns them and clients that have individual permissions are not reported. The method therefore returns wrong data for callers that filter client listings by granted permission.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NPE when the "Clients" resource-type resource does not exist

In `hasPermission(ClientModel, String)`, when no per-client resource exists the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)`, which can legitimately return `null` (it returns null when the realm's `adminPermissionsEnabled` flag is off, or when the `Clients` resource simply does not exist in the resource server, e.g. a realm whose admin-permissions client was initialized before the `Clients` resource type was added). The returned value is immediately passed to `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and later to `new ResourcePermission(resource, resource.getScopes(), server)` without a null check, producing a NullPointerException / HTTP 500 on ordinary admin endpoints such as GET/PUT /clients/{id}. A null check returning `false` is needed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
Client/role/group removal breaks when both ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ and V2 are enabled

The removal listener is now guarded by `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)`, but `management()` returns `MgmtPermissionsV2` whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled. With both features enabled (they are independent flags), a `ClientModel.ClientRemovedEvent` now calls `MgmtPermissionsV2.clients()` -> `ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(...)`, which throws `UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2")`. The event listener runs inside the removal transaction, so deleting a client fails with a server error instead of cleaning up V1 permission policies. The listener should select the V1 management implementation explicitly (or the V2 implementation must tolerate these calls).

Javadoc on require* methods documents a return value for void methods

`requireView()` (line 95-98) and `requireViewClientScopes()` (line 100-103) are documented as "Returns {@code true} if {@link #canView()} returns {@code true}" / "...if {@link #canViewClientScopes()} returns {@code true}", but both methods are `void` and throw ForbiddenException when the check fails, like the other `require*` methods in this interface. The docs should state the throwing behaviour, otherwise implementers/callers are misled about the contract.

New map-roles-client-scope scope and client-scope permissions are untested

The PR adds the scopes `configure`, `map-roles`, `map-roles-composite`, `map-roles-client-scope` and the client-scope related evaluations (`canManage(ClientScopeModel)`, `canView(ClientScopeModel)`, `canManageClientScopes()`), but the new tests only cover MANAGE, CONFIGURE, VIEW, MAP_ROLES and MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE. `canMapClientScopeRoles` / `MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE` and the ClientScopeModel-based checks have no coverage, so regressions in those code paths (including the ones that intentionally differ from V1) would go unnoticed.

No upgrade path for realms whose admin-permissions client was already initialized

`init()` creates the authorization scopes and the per-resource-type "all" resources only once, when the admin permissions client is first created (it returns early if `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`). Realms that already enabled ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 before this change therefore have neither the new `Clients` resource nor the new scopes `configure`, `map-roles-client-scope`, `map-roles-composite`. For those realms, creating a Clients permission fails (`getOrCreateResource` throws `ModelException("No scopes found.")` when a scope is missing) and client permission evaluation hits the missing `Clients` resource. Either a migration that adds missing scopes/resources, or lazy creation on demand, is required.

Overridden methods throwing UnsupportedOperationException turn 403/legacy paths into 500s

`canExchangeTo`, `isPermissionsEnabled`, `getPermissions`, `resource` and the `*Permission(ClientModel)` methods all throw `UnsupportedOperationException`. These are still reached at runtime when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled: the token-exchange flow calls `AdminPermissions.management(session, realm).clients().canExchangeTo(...)` to decide whether an exchange to another client is allowed, and the `/clients/{id}/management/permissions` admin endpoints call `isPermissionsEnabled`/`setPermissionsEnabled` (the latter only requires the V1 feature, which can be enabled simultaneously). The result is an HTTP 500 instead of the previous Forbidden/clean response. These methods should return a safe value (e.g. `false`) or the call sites must be guarded.

getResourceName not extended for the Clients resource type

`getResourceName` only resolves human-readable names for the `Users` resource type. For the newly added `Clients` resource type it falls through to `resource.getDisplayName()`, which is null for resources created by `getOrCreateResource` (only name=clientId-UUID and owner are set). Consequently the admin REST/console representation of a client permission shows a null/empty resource name instead of the client's clientId, and there is no "All clients" label analogous to "All users".

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Documented update-compatibility command appends --features, overriding the user's feature set

The `updatecompatibility` macro now renders every command in the Update Compatibility guide as `bin/kc.sh update-compatibility <sub> ... --features=rolling-updates`. `--features` is a single, replacing list, not additive, so a user who copies this command loses all other features they have configured (via `KC_FEATURES`, keycloak.conf or the image build). Since the guide simultaneously warns that "omitting any configuration options will result in incomplete metadata", the documented command produces metadata for a different feature set than the running deployment. In addition, `features` is a build-time option, so for an optimized distribution/image passing it on the CLI is rejected or forces re-augmentation. The guide should instruct users to add `rolling-updates` to their existing feature list (or enable it at build time) rather than show a bare `--features=rolling-updates`.

Exit-code contract changed: 4 no longer means "recreate required"

`RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE` is changed from 4 to 3 and 4 is reused for the new `FEATURE_DISABLED` result. These constants are the documented, scriptable contract of `kc.sh update-compatibility check` (the guide explicitly tells users to rely only on the exit code). Any existing consumer that hardcodes 4 as "recreate upgrade needed" – including automation pipelines and any operator/job code that inspects the terminated container's exit code – will now silently interpret "the rolling-updates feature is disabled" as "perform a recreate upgrade", and will no longer recognise a real recreate result (3). No non-documentation consumer was updated in this PR; please confirm every reader of these codes uses the constants, and consider picking an unused code (e.g. 5) for the new condition instead of recycling 4.

New FEATURE_DISABLED exit code is not covered by tests

`testFeatureNotEnabled` only asserts the stderr text and only for the `metadata` subcommand. The newly introduced exit code 4 (`CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED`), which is now part of the documented contract and which also collides with the previous meaning of exit code 4 (recreate upgrade), is never asserted; neither is the feature-disabled path of the `check` subcommand. Also no test asserts the new recreate exit code 3. A future renumbering or a regression in the feature gate would not be caught. Add assertions on `exitCode()` for both subcommands with the feature disabled, and for the recreate result.

Operator CAUTION about required feature is overbroad/ambiguous

The new CAUTION states unconditionally that "the feature `rolling-updates` must be enabled. Otherwise, the {project_name} Operator will fail." That contradicts the behaviour exercised by `UpgradeTest`, which enables the feature only when `spec.update.strategy` is set and still runs successfully (default/unset strategy) without the feature. As written, readers will think the feature is mandatory for every Keycloak CR managed by the Operator. The text should state precisely when the feature is required (e.g. only when `spec.update` is used) and what "fail" means (CR in error status, reconciliation error).

Test replaces instead of appending the CR's enabled features

`setEnabledFeatures(List.of(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey()))` unconditionally overwrites whatever `spec.features.enabled` the base test deployment provides. If the shared test CR template ever enables another feature, it is silently dropped here and the test would exercise a different configuration than intended (or fail for an unrelated reason). The existing list should be read and extended with `rolling-updates`.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() grants group-management rights to admins that only have the `view` scope

`GroupPermissionsV2.canManage()` returns `true` when the caller has either `AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW` **or** `MANAGE` on the all-groups resource. `canManage()` (no argument) is the check behind `GroupPermissionEvaluator.requireManage()`, which `GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup()` uses to authorize group creation. Consequently an admin granted only a read-only `view` permission on `Groups` can create top-level groups, a privilege escalation. The group-scoped variant `canManage(GroupModel)` correctly requires only `MANAGE`, confirming `VIEW` here is a copy/paste mistake. There is also no test asserting that a `view`-only permission is rejected for write operations (`testViewGroups` only exercises reads), so the bug is not caught.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() uses authorization Resource IDs instead of group IDs

Group resources in the FGAP v2 schema are stored with `name == group.getId()` (see `AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup`/`getOrCreateResource`), while `Resource.getId()` is a separate generated UUID. This method (a) calls `hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...)`, and `hasPermission` resolves the argument via `resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)`, so the lookup always misses and the evaluation silently falls back to the all-groups resource — per-group `view-members`/`manage-members` permissions are therefore never detected here; and (b) adds `groupResource.getId()` to the returned set, whereas callers (`UsersResource.searchForUser` via `session.setAttribute(UserModel.GROUPS, ...)`, and `UsersResource.getUsersCount(..., groupIds)`) expect group IDs and match them against group membership. Result: `GET /users/count` returns 0 (or wrong values) for an admin whose only visibility comes from group `view-members` permissions, inconsistent with `GET /users`, and the group-id filter pushed into the user query can never match. The V1 implementation correctly uses `resource.getName()`. Note also that `findByType(server, "Groups", ...)` returns the all-groups resource itself, whose name is `"Groups"` and is not a group ID, so it would be added to the set as a bogus group ID if an all-groups permission exists.

false_positives.candidate:
Feature check moved from event time to listener-registration time

`registerListener` now evaluates `Profile.isFeatureEnabled(ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ)` once, when the provider event listener is registered during factory initialization, instead of on each event. If the profile is not yet fully resolved at registration time (or registration happens before feature configuration), the listener is never registered and role/client/group permission cleanup on removal silently stops working for the whole server lifetime, with no error. Keeping the check inside `onEvent` (or asserting profile availability at registration) avoids this ordering dependency.

Javadoc on requireManageMembers / getGroupIdsWithViewPermission is wrong

The javadoc for `requireManageMembers(GroupModel)` states it throws when `canManageMembership(GroupModel)` returns false, but the implementation checks `canManageMembers(GroupModel)` — a copy/paste error that misleads implementors of the interface. Additionally `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission()` is documented as returning a "Stream of IDs" while it returns a `Set<String>`.

No cleanup of group authorization resources/permissions when a group is deleted under FGAP v2

`AdminPermissions.registerListener` only registers the `GroupRemovedEvent` handler when the v1 `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ` feature is enabled, and `GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled` throws `UnsupportedOperationException` anyway. With the new Groups resource type, deleting a group leaves the authorization `Resource` named with the group id plus every scope permission referencing it orphaned in the admin-permissions client forever. Beyond growing stale data, these orphan entries show up when listing permissions/resources in the admin API (where `AdminPermissionsSchema.getResourceName` cannot resolve them) and must be deleted manually. A removal hook (analogous to the v1 listener) should delete the group resource and its permissions.

No migration path: existing admin-permissions clients never get the Groups resource and group scopes

`init()` returns early when `realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null`, so realms that already enabled FGAP v2 before this change keep an admin-permissions client without the `Groups` resource and without the new `manage-membership`, `manage-members`, `view-members` scopes. In such realms creating a group permission fails in `getOrCreateResource` with `ModelException("No scopes found.")` (the scope lookup at line 125 returns null) and `GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission` gets a null all-groups resource. Either a migration that adds the missing resource/scopes or lazy creation is needed.

Possible NullPointerException when the all-groups resource cannot be resolved

In `hasPermission`, when no per-group resource is found the code falls back to `AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(...)`, which returns `null` if the realm does not support the authorization schema (e.g. `realm.isAdminPermissionsEnabled() == false`) or if the `Groups` resource does not exist (realms whose admin-permissions client was created before this change). The returned value is used without a null check in `policyStore.findByResource(server, resource)` and `resource.getScopes()`, producing an NPE / HTTP 500 on ordinary admin endpoints (group listing, user search) instead of a clean `false`. Note `MgmtPermissionsV2` is selected purely on the `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` feature flag, so a realm with the feature on but admin permissions turned off (while the admin-permissions client still exists) reaches this path.

Removal of public static ModelToRepresentation.searchGroupModelsByAttributes breaks compiled extensions

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() aborts the shutdown loop, leaving the remaining processes unterminated

In `join()`, when the deadline has passed the loop `break`s out before reaching the `process.terminate()` call for the remaining entries of `self.processes`. With more than one flusher process, a timed-out join therefore terminates only the processes iterated before the deadline expired; the rest are left running and continue flushing segments while the consumer is shutting down/rebalancing. (Additionally, `remaining_time` is computed but never used, and the `terminate()` call itself is dead for spawn processes because of the same `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` problem.) Terminate every process unconditionally after the wait loop.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: breaking out of the loop when the deadline expires skips the termination call for the remaining flusher processes in the list, leaving them running after shutdown.

false_positives.candidate:
New multi-process flusher test only asserts bookkeeping, never exercises flushing across shards

`test_flusher_processes_limit` creates 4 partitions with `flusher_processes=2` but never submits a message and never asserts that segments from all 4 shards are produced. It only checks `len(flusher.processes)`, `max_processes`, `num_processes` and the total shard count. The behaviour this PR actually changes — several shards being flushed by one worker, and all shards being covered by the shard->process mapping — is untested. Consider submitting spans for each partition and asserting that one produced message per shard arrives, and that `process_to_shards_map` is a partition of `assigned_shards` (no duplicates/omissions).

Dead method `_create_process_for_shard` left behind

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). Dead code that duplicates restart logic is a maintenance hazard — a future caller would restart a whole process group from a single shard id. Remove it.

Class docstring claims one process per shard and documents a non-existent param

The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the number of processes is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))`, and the consumer CLI defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, so the normal configuration is a single process handling all shards. The docstring also still documents `:param topic:` which is not an argument, and does not document the new `max_processes` argument. This misleads operators about the default parallelism.

A new SpansBuffer (and its Redis clients) is created in the parent on every restart without releasing the old one

`_create_process_for_shards` constructs a fresh `SpansBuffer(shards)` and stores it in `self.buffers[process_index]`, overwriting the previous instance. The parent process keeps using these buffers for `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()`, so each unhealthy-process restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process) leaves the previous buffer's Redis connections unclosed in the parent. Reuse the existing buffer for the process index, or close the old one before replacing it.

false_positives.candidate:
get_environment_info triggers a per-issue recommended-event lookup during PR comment generation

`get_environment_info()` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in a merged-PR comment. That helper performs a search/snuba query plus a nodestore fetch per issue, so generating a comment for the top 5 issues now issues up to 5 extra remote queries inside the webhook/task path that previously only read `issue.culprit` from the already-loaded model. This adds latency and external load to every PR comment, and the broad `except Exception` means failures are invisible apart from an info log. Consider batching the environment lookup (or deriving it from data already fetched for the issue list).

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES filter only applies while searching

`sortedAndFilteredAttributes` returns `sorted` early when `searchQuery` is empty, so the newly added `HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES` exclusion (`is_segment`, `project_id`, `received`) is only applied once the user types something. In the default (no search) state those attributes are still shown, which is the opposite of the intent and makes the list inconsistent as soon as a user starts/clears a search. The hidden-attribute filter should be applied to the base list, independently of the search term.

Hook can now return undefined attributes where it previously always returned a TagCollection

The hook was rewritten to return `attributes: isFetching ? previous : data` from `useQuery`. `data` is `undefined` whenever the query errors, is disabled (`enabled` false), or has not run, and `previous` is also `undefined` on the first render — whereas the old implementation always derived a concrete `TagCollection` object (`result.data ?? []` reduced into `{}`). Consumers that do `Object.keys(attributes)` or spread the value (e.g. the filter-key sections / search query builder tag collections) will throw on error or while the hook is disabled. Default to `{}` (or make the undefined case explicit for all callers).

Attribute-keys query key omits the organization

`queryKey` is `['use-trace-item-attribute-keys', queryOptions]`, and `makeTraceItemAttributeKeysQueryOptions` only contains item type, attribute type, project ids and the datetime range — the organization slug used to build the request URL is not part of the key. Two organizations with the same project ids/date range would share a cache entry, so attribute keys from one org can be served for another after an org switch within the same session. Include the organization slug (or the full URL) in the query key.

One invalid report rejects the entire batch

The POST handler returns 422 for the whole request as soon as any single report in the array fails validation, discarding the valid reports in the same batch. Browsers send reports in batches and will keep retrying the same (permanently invalid) payload, so a single malformed report from one page permanently blocks collection of the rest of that batch. Consider skipping/counting invalid reports and still returning 200 for the valid ones.

Coverage for the application/reports+json content type was removed

The previous test posted with `content_type="application/reports+json"` (the content type browsers actually use for the Reporting API) and asserted the request body was logged. After the refactor every success-path test posts with the default content type, so `BrowserReportsJSONParser` — the only reason the custom parser class exists — is no longer exercised by any test. A regression in the parser media type would silently break real browser reports while the suite stays green.

Custom cell renderers fall back on any falsy return, not just undefined

Both `renderDefaultHeadCell` and `renderDefaultBodyCell` do `const cell = render...(); if (cell) return cell;`. The documented contract (see tableWidgetVisualization.stories.tsx and the prop JSDoc) is that returning `undefined` triggers the fallback renderer. With a truthiness check, a custom renderer that legitimately returns `null` (render nothing), `''`, or `0` will be silently replaced by the default renderer, which is not what the docs promise and is hard to debug. Compare against `undefined` explicitly.

false_positives.candidate:
Java MessageFormat choice/placeholder syntax introduced into an i18next-consumed message bundle

This file is consumed by the account console (i18next), where parameters are interpolated with the `{{n}}` syntax – every other parameterized key in this file uses it (e.g. `error-invalid-length='{{0}}' must have a length between {{1}} and {{2}}.`). The new value `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.` uses Java `MessageFormat` single-brace placeholders plus a `choice` format, neither of which i18next understands. As a result the user will see the literal text `{0}`, `{1}`, `{2}` and `{2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}` instead of actual values. The previous `{{0}} ... value(s)` form worked; only the server-side (Java) bundles should use choice formats.

Admin console message switched to Java MessageFormat syntax that i18next cannot render

`error-invalid-multivalued-size` was changed to `Attribute {0} must have at least {1} and at most {2} {2,choice,0#values|1#value|1<values}.`. This bundle is rendered by the admin console through i18next, which interpolates `{{n}}` (see neighbouring keys such as `error-invalid-length` in the same file) and has no support for `MessageFormat` choice formats. The message will be displayed with raw `{0}`/`{1}`/`{2}` and the whole `{2,choice,...}` block visible to administrators.

Diff trimming can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException while reporting a violation The common-prefix (`start`) and common-suffix (`end`) scans are independent, so the two regions can overlap and `start + end` can exceed the length of `value` or `sanitized`. `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` then fails with StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. A concrete example: value `x

y` sanitized to `x
y` gives start=5, end=5, so `sanitized.substring(5, 1)` throws. Instead of a readable "Illegal HTML in key ..." message the plugin crashes with an unrelated runtime exception, hiding the actual problem. Clamp `end` to `min(len) - start` before building the substrings.

Missing English reference bundle aborts the build with an opaque RuntimeException

The English counterpart path is derived purely by string replacement (`resources-community` -> `resources`, `_<locale>.properties` -> `_en.properties`). If that file does not exist (community-only theme/locale layout, a bundle whose name does not follow the `_xx.properties` convention, or a locale containing digits which the `[a-zA-Z-_]*` class does not match), the constructor throws an unchecked RuntimeException out of `verify()`, which declares `MojoExecutionException`. The Maven run then fails with a raw stack trace rather than a diagnosable plugin error, and the file is not verified. Either skip verification when no reference bundle exists or wrap the failure in MojoExecutionException with the computed path.

Anchor-mismatch error message does not identify the file or key

`messages.add("Didn't find anchor tag " + matcher.group() + " in original string")` omits both the properties file and the message key, unlike the HTML message a few lines below which includes them. With hundreds of bundles verified in one build, a contributor cannot tell which translation to fix. The already-passed `key` parameter is unused; include it and `file` in the message.

Unescaping HTML entities turns safe escaped markup into reported violations

`normalizeValue` runs `unescapeHtml4` on the raw property value, so a translation that deliberately contains escaped markup (e.g. `<div>`) becomes real markup before sanitization. The sanitizer strips it and the key is then reported as "Illegal HTML" even though the original value is harmless literal text. This produces false positives that contributors can only work around by rewording the message.

Verification compares sanitizer output verbatim, flagging harmless HTML formatting as illegal The check requires the message to be byte-identical to the OWASP sanitizer's re-serialized output. Semantically identical markup that the sanitizer normalizes differently (for example `
` vs `
`, attribute quoting/order, or whitespace inside tags) is reported as "Illegal HTML", which is both misleading and brittle – this is why ~20 translation files in this PR had to be rewritten from `
` to `
`. Any future contribution using the other spelling will fail CI with a security-sounding error. Consider comparing the set of allowed elements/attributes, or normalizing both sides through the sanitizer before comparison.

Italian text inserted into the Lithuanian login bundle

`loginTotpStep1=Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:` is Italian text in the Lithuanian login messages. It replaces the former Lithuanian sentence, so the OTP setup screen for the `lt` locale now shows Italian.

No test asserting that valid messages produce no findings

All four tests only assert that a violation is reported. Nothing verifies the negative case: that a bundle whose translation legitimately contains the allowed elements (`br`, `p`, `strong`, `b`), the same anchor as the English source, placeholders such as `{0}`/`{{0}}`, or a `{n,choice,...}` block yields an empty message list. Given how much special-casing `normalizeValue`/`santizeAnchors` contain, false positives (which would break the whole themes build) are the most likely regression and are currently untested.

In `isAccessTokenId(String expectedGrantShortcut)` the check is `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.
