As written, the two bugs cancel out and every event with a well-formed token id passes regardless of the grant shortcut, so all the new `expectCodeToToken`/`expectRefresh`/`expectDeviceCodeToToken`/`expectAuthReqIdToToken` assertions verify nothing about the grant type (and would start failing with false negatives as soon as either half is fixed).

false_positives.candidate:
New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

`getShortcut()` is added as an abstract method on the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` SPI interface. Any third-party/custom grant type factory compiled against a previous release no longer satisfies the interface and will fail with `AbstractMethodError` (or not compile) once deployed - and because `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates all grant factories and calls `getShortcut()`, the failure happens at server start. Providing a `default` implementation (e.g. deriving a shortcut or returning null and handling it) would keep the SPI backwards compatible.

Removal of Context copy constructor is a breaking change

The `public Context(Context context)` copy constructor was deleted from `OAuth2GrantType.Context`. Subclasses outside this repository (and any code that wrapped a Context, e.g. token-exchange contexts) use it; after this change they can no longer compile/link, and there is no replacement that copies an existing Context. If the copy semantics are no longer needed internally, the constructor should still be kept (deprecated) or an equivalent copy path provided.

Context constructor now NPEs on null formParams

The constructor now dereferences `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. Previously `formParams` was only stored, so a null value was tolerated by this constructor. Any caller constructing a Context without form parameters now gets a NullPointerException at construction time instead of later (or never). A null-guard (`formParams == null ? null : formParams.getFirst(...)`) would preserve the previous contract.

Decoding throws IllegalArgumentException for any token id containing ':' in an unexpected format

`getTokenContextFromTokenId` treats any id containing ':' as encoded and then throws `IllegalArgumentException` if the prefix is not exactly 6 characters or if a shortcut is unknown. Token ids produced by a different/older encoder, by a custom `TokenContextEncoderProvider`, or by a federated/externally issued token could legitimately contain ':' and would cause an unhandled runtime exception (HTTP 500) in whatever endpoint decodes the id, instead of degrading to an UNKNOWN context like the no-colon case does. Also the message "Expected length of 6" refers to the prefix, not the token id that is printed, which is confusing.

Lazy shortcut cache refresh can NPE and bypasses duplicate-shortcut validation

`getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut` lazily insert into the `ConcurrentHashMap`s for grant types discovered after `postInit`. If a (custom) `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` returns null, `grantsByShortcuts.put(null, grantType)` throws NullPointerException; the same happens in `postInit`, failing server startup with an opaque error instead of a message naming the offending factory. In addition, the duplicate-shortcut consistency check performed in `postInit` is not applied on these lazy inserts, so a newly deployed grant with a colliding shortcut silently overwrites an existing mapping, making decoded grant types wrong.

Session type derived from clientSession.getUserSession() instead of the user session already available

`getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` resolves the user session via `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and immediately dereferences it. `TokenManager.initToken`, the only caller, already has a non-null `userSession` parameter it uses for exactly the same persistence-state check. For client session contexts whose client session is not (yet) attached to a user session this call yields a NullPointerException during access token creation. Passing/using the known `userSession` removes the risk and the redundant lookup.

Externally visible jti format change without upgrade documentation

Access token `jti` values change from a bare UUID to `<6-char prefix>:<uuid>` (and the same value is reported in the `token_id` event detail). Relying parties, log pipelines and tests that assume `jti` is a UUID (or validate its length/charset) will break. The PR contains no upgrading-guide/release-note entry describing this behaviour change or the new `tokenContextEncoder` SPI.

Unchecked Optional.get() breaks login form for user-storage recovery codes

`RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` returns an `Optional`, and the result is dereferenced with `.get()` without an `isPresent()` check. With this PR, recovery codes can now be owned by a user-storage provider: `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator.configuredFor()` only asks `isConfiguredFor(RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.TYPE)` (a `CredentialInputValidator` call), while `getCredential()` relies on the provider also exposing the credential through `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`. A provider that validates the credential but does not expose it (a very common combination, e.g. a provider implementing only `CredentialInputValidator`/`CredentialInputUpdater`) will make the authenticator render this bean, and the empty `Optional` throws `NoSuchElementException`, resulting in a 500 error page instead of a login challenge. The same applies to `getNextRecoveryAuthnCode().get()` on line 21. Both need a graceful fallback/error path.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same core issue: calling `Optional.get()` directly on the result of `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)` without checking `isPresent()`, which can throw a `NoSuchElementException`. Although the golden comment briefly mentions raw List deserialization, the primary issue described is the unsafe Optional access, which the candidate explains in great detail.

false_positives.candidate:
Pre-existing local recovery-codes credential is left valid after codes are stored in user storage

`createRecoveryCodesCredential()` calls `user.credentialManager().updateCredential(...)` and, when the user-storage provider handles it, skips creating/replacing the local credential entirely. Any previously stored *local* recovery-codes credential for that user is neither removed nor overwritten. This is exactly the upgrade scenario this PR targets: a federated user who configured recovery codes before the provider supported the type keeps the old local credential, and `SubjectCredentialManager.isValid()` will still accept those old codes via the local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider`. Re-generating recovery codes must invalidate the previous set; here the old codes stay valid indefinitely. Additionally `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential()` now prefers the federated credential, so the stale local credential is invisible in the UI while remaining usable for authentication.

User label and generation timestamp are dropped when codes are stored in user storage

The credential handed to the user-storage provider is built as `new UserCredentialModel("", type, recoveryCodesJson)`, i.e. only the raw codes are transferred; the `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel` (which carries the user-entered label from the `userLabel` form field and the `generatedAt` timestamp) is used only on the local-storage branch. Consequently, for federated users the label the user typed in the required-action form is silently discarded and cannot be shown in the account/admin console. The new value format (a JSON array of raw codes in `getChallengeResponse()` on update, versus a single raw code on validation) is also completely undocumented in the method javadoc, so third-party provider authors cannot implement `updateCredential` for this type correctly.

Exhausted federated recovery-codes credential is removed from the wrong store

`getCredential()` can now return a credential coming from the user-storage provider (via `getFederatedCredentialsStream()`), but when `allCodesUsed()` is true the code still calls `authenticatedUser.credentialManager().removeStoredCredentialById(recoveryCodeCredentialModel.getId())`, which only addresses Keycloak's local credential store. For a federated credential this is a no-op (and the id may even be null, since providers typically build the model with `createFromValues(...)` which does not set an id), so the exhausted credential is left in the user storage. true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate index builds for the same key

BuildIndex previously held `b.cacheMu` for the whole function, which serialized builds and guaranteed that only one index per NamespacedResource was ever constructed. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. Nothing prevents two goroutines from calling BuildIndex for the same key concurrently (e.g. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does an unsynchronized GetIndex-then-build, and it is reachable from both the watch-event handler and concurrent Search calls). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, so the second call fails with a 'path already exists' error and the request errors out; (2) duplicated full index builds waste CPU/IO; (3) the loser's bleve index is overwritten in the cache and never closed, leaking file handles/memory. If the goal is finer-grained locking, a per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed rather than no mutual exclusion at all.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact same concurrency problem described in the golden comment: narrowing the scope of `b.cacheMu` in `BuildIndex` to only the final map assignment allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same index for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map under `b.cacheMu` from arbitrary goroutines (index builds triggered by watch events or search requests). Concurrent map read and map write is a fatal, unrecoverable Go runtime error ('concurrent map read and map write') that crashes the process. Previously this was partially masked because BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole duration; with the finer locking, writes happen far more often and at unpredictable times. TotalDocs should take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same concurrency bug: `TotalDocs` iterates over `b.cache` without synchronization/locking while `BuildIndex` can concurrently write to `b.cache` (triggered by watch events), leading to a fatal concurrent map read/write panic in Go.

false_positives.candidate:
errgroup goroutines share the outer `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables (data race, lost errors)

Inside `group.Go(...)` the code does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigning to the `err` declared in the enclosing function, and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed`. With `initWorkers > 1` these are concurrent unsynchronized writes: a genuine data race (will be flagged by `-race`) and, worse, one goroutine's error can be clobbered by another goroutine before `group.Wait()` returns, and `err = group.Wait()` can be overwritten by a still-running assignment. Since this function now runs at server construction and its error aborts startup, misreporting matters. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic counter.

Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the server context and background goroutines

`NewResourceServer` creates `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` and stores `cancel` on the server. When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, the function returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during Init — the storage backend's watch poller started by `searchSupport.init` via `WatchWriteEvents`, and the broadcaster/watcher if `initWatcher` partially succeeded — keeps running against a context that is never cancelled, leaking goroutines, DB connections and the context itself for the lifetime of the process. Call `cancel()` (or `s.Stop`) on the error path.

Removing per-request Init() checks means requests are still served after Stop()

`Stop` communicates shutdown by setting `s.initErr = "service is stopping"` / `"service is stopped"`, and the only thing that ever read `initErr` on the request path were the `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil` guards that this PR deleted from Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/History/Origin/IsHealthy/PutBlob/GetBlob. After this change, requests arriving after `Stop()` no longer fail fast; they fall through to a backend whose context has been cancelled, producing confusing 'context canceled' errors (or, for blob/diagnostics paths, operating on torn-down state) instead of the intended shutdown error. Either keep a cheap state check at the entry of the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` shutdown signalling in `Stop`.

Index build now runs synchronously in the constructor with an uncancellable, unbounded context

`s.Init(ctx)` is invoked from `NewResourceServer` with a `context.Background()`-derived context that has no deadline, and it performs the full search index build (`searchSupport.init`, which lists every resource of every namespace). Constructing the resource server therefore blocks Grafana/storage-server startup for as long as indexing takes, with no timeout and no way for the caller to cancel; a slow or unresponsive database makes startup hang indefinitely rather than failing or degrading. Consider a bounded context or kicking the index build off asynchronously while keeping the lifecycle/backend init synchronous.

Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close and then reused after rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, but the per-assignment strategy's `close()`/`terminate()`/`join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the worker threads. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on every partition revocation (rebalance), and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again for the new assignment. On that second call `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes, so a strategy is built around a pool whose worker threads are dead and whose queues are shut down: every `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` swallows in its generic `except Exception` handler and then marks the offset as completed. The consumer will therefore silently drop all messages while still committing their offsets after any rebalance. The pool must be created per assignment (or re-created in `create_with_partitions`) rather than shared across strategy lifetimes.

Unbounded queues mean no backpressure, contradicting the documented guarantee

Each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `arroyo.processing.strategies.abstract.MessageRejected`. As a result the strategy accepts messages from the Kafka consumer as fast as they arrive regardless of worker progress: work items (which also retain the full `Message`/`KafkaPayload`) and their tracked offsets accumulate in memory without bound when a group's processing is slow, which is exactly the scenario this PR is meant to address. This also contradicts the class docstring ("Natural backpressure when queues fill up"). A bounded queue plus `MessageRejected` on `queue.Full` is needed for arroyo to actually throttle consumption.

close() stops the commit thread before draining queues, losing committable offsets

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, and only then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which drains the remaining queued items (`shutdown(immediate=False)` lets queued work finish). Any item processed during that drain completes its offset after the only thread that commits offsets has already exited, so those offsets are never committed. On restart/rebalance all of that work is reprocessed. Additionally `join(timeout)` ignores the supplied timeout and just calls `close()`, so arroyo's shutdown deadline is not honoured. The order should be: stop accepting work, drain the queues, perform a final `get_committable_offsets()` + commit, then stop the commit thread.

Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`commit_offsets` (passed as `commit_function`) is called from `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the arroyo `StreamProcessor` concurrently polls and commits on the main thread. The `Commit` callable given to `create_with_partitions` stages/commits offsets on the shared consumer state and is expected to be called from the processing (main) thread; calling it concurrently races with the processor's own offset staging/commit and with partition revocation (where it can raise `ConsumerError` for unassigned partitions, silently swallowed by the loop's `except Exception`). This can produce lost or incorrect offset commits. Offsets should be collected by the background workers and committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the main thread instead.

A single missing offset permanently blocks all commits for the partition

`get_committable_offsets()` walks offsets contiguously from `last_committed + 1` and `break`s on the first offset that is not present in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous as seen by a consumer (transactional/control records, compaction, or any message that never reaches `submit` because an upstream wrapper such as the DLQ/stale-message wrapper consumed it). If one offset in the sequence is never added, that partition can never advance its commit point: `all_offsets` grows without bound and the consumer group lag never decreases, causing full reprocessing of everything after the gap on restart. There needs to be a mechanism to advance past offsets that will never be seen (e.g. seed the committed position from the assignment and treat unknown offsets below the current max as done).

Generic exception handler in submit() drops messages and commits their offsets

`submit()` wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one `try/except Exception`; on any failure (including a failing `grouping_fn`, a `FilteredPayload` payload which trips the `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` in `decode_payload`, or `queue.ShutDown` from a shut-down pool) it logs and then marks the offset as both added and completed. The message is silently discarded and its offset is committed, so the data is lost with no DLQ and no visible failure other than a log line. Expected non-processable cases (filtered payloads, decode failures) should be handled explicitly, and unexpected enqueue failures should either raise (so arroyo can DLQ/stop) rather than ack the offset.

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys hash into exactly all 3 queues (`len(queue_indices) == 3`). `get_queue_for_group` uses `hash()` on a `str`, which is salted per interpreter run (PYTHONHASHSEED), so there is a small but non-zero chance (~0.1%) that one bucket receives no key and the test fails for unrelated reasons. Every `OrderedQueueWorker` emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` with only an `identifier` tag, so all N workers (20 by default) report the depth of their own queue under the same metric series. Either skip caching the denial when the decision depended on the folder tree, or invalidate/refresh the folder tree on the fallback path.

Every non-cached denial triggers a full permission re-query and an unbounded cache entry

The cache read was removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` now falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (DB query for basic role, teams and permissions) whenever the cached scope map does not grant the requested resource. Combined with a denial cache keyed by `(namespace, user, action, name, parentFolder)`, any sequence of checks over distinct resource names the user cannot access produces one DB permission query per distinct name, and one new cache entry per distinct name. For bulk authorization (e.g. checking many dashboards during a search) or for a caller passing arbitrary names, this is a significant DB-load amplification versus the previous behaviour (single cached scope map), and the local cache grows without bound until TTL expiry. Consider rate-limiting the re-query (e.g. a short "recently refreshed" marker per user+action) instead of re-querying on every miss.

permissionCacheUsage metric records a miss when the cache was actually hit

When `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeds but the cached scope map does not grant access, control falls through to line 137 and increments `permissionCacheUsage` with label `"false"` (miss), even though the permission cache was hit. Because the per-function metric increments were removed from `getUserPermissions`, this is now the only accounting point, so cache hit-rate dashboards will systematically under-report hits for denied checks and make the new caching behaviour impossible to evaluate.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

true_positives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OAuth `state` is the deterministic pipeline signature, so the state check gives no CSRF protection

The authorize redirect uses `state = pipeline.signature` and the callback only checks `request.GET.get("state") != pipeline.signature`. The pipeline signature is deterministic and not user/session specific — the new tests hardcode the same value `9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3` for different users and organizations (`test_github_installed_on_another_org`, `test_github_user_mismatch`, `test_github_prevent_install_until_pending_deletion_is_complete`). true_positives.matched_candidate:

true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: accessing `integration.metadata['sender']['login']` without checking if the `'sender'` key exists, which causes a `KeyError` when `sender` metadata was not set during integration creation.

false_positives.candidate:

`safe_urlopen(...)` (line 423) and `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` (line 434) are called without exception handling. `get_user_info` performs an HTTP request and raises `ApiError`/`ApiHostError` on non-2xx or network failures (e.g. revoked token, GitHub outage, rate limiting), and `safe_urlopen` raises on connection errors. The result is an unhandled 500 in the install popup rather than the intended `github-integration-failed.html` page, with no log line to diagnose it. Wrap both calls and fall back to `error(request, self.active_organization)` (plus a log).

This test previously asserted `b"The GitHub installation could not be found."`, covering the `ApiError(404) -> IntegrationError` branch in `GitHubIntegrationProvider.build_integration`. gettext applied to a runtime variable breaks string extraction for the short error messages

`error()` wraps its `error_short` argument at call time with `_(error_short)`. Because the argument is a variable rather than a literal inside the `_()` call, `makemessages` cannot extract strings like "GitHub installation pending deletion." or "Github installed on another Sentry organization." anymore (previously they were literals inside `_()`), so these user-facing strings will silently stop being translated. Pass already-lazy/translated values from the call sites instead of translating the variable.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation on update is decided from the organization-aware wrapper, so it depends on transient organization state

`update()` passes `idpById` (obtained from `getById()`, which returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`) into `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the organization provider for the realm) is disabled, even though the stored IDP row is enabled. As a result `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` can evaluate to `false` for an IDP that *is* present in the cached login ID sets (the DB query behind `getForLogin` only filters on the IDP's own `enabled` flag, not on the organization state). Note the inconsistency with `remove()`, which correctly uses the unwrapped `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`; `update()` should likewise use the raw stored model (or compare only the IDP's own fields).

The test only removes `idp-alias-1` (a disabled provider, i.e. not login-eligible) and only creates `idp-alias-20` with `hideOnLogin=true`, so both assertions verify that the login caches are *not* invalidated. The newly added `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(model)` in `create()` and `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` in `remove()` are therefore never exercised in their positive branch: a regression that drops either call (leaving the login caches stale after adding or deleting a login-eligible broker) would not be caught. Add a case that creates an enabled, non-hidden provider and one that removes a login-eligible provider, and assert the `*.idp.login.*` entries disappear.

The search key is always derived from `organizationId`, but for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the delegate ignores `organizationId` entirely (it forces `ORGANIZATION_ID=null`). Any caller invoking `getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, someOrgId)` therefore creates a distinct search key for a logically identical result, and each new key triggers `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` plus a full re-query before being merged back. For `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL`, one cached `IdentityProviderListQuery` per realm accumulates one entry per organization id ever queried, with no bound or pruning, so memory grows with the number of organizations that are used for login. Consider using an empty search key for REALM_ONLY and bounding/keying per-organization results separately.

getForLogin now returns providers in non-deterministic order

The cached implementation collects internal ids into a `HashSet` and returns `new HashSet<>(...).stream()`, so the order of the returned providers is unspecified and can differ between calls/JVMs. Before this change the stream order followed the underlying query order (realm-level providers first, then organization providers, in the order produced by JPA). Callers that rely on a stable order or that take `findFirst()` on the result will now behave unpredictably; the login page happens to re-sort, but the SPI contract change affects every other consumer. Either preserve ordering (e.g. `LinkedHashSet`/list) or document that the order is undefined.

The new predicate does `Boolean.parseBoolean(idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC))` whenever `idp.getOrganizationId() != null`. `IdentityProviderModel.getConfig()` is not guaranteed to be non-null (it can be set to `null` via `setConfig`, e.g. when a representation without a config is converted), so this can throw a `NullPointerException` from `create()`/`update()` in the Infinispan provider, which now calls the predicate on the caller-supplied model. true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

If N goroutines reach this point concurrently at startup (the common case, since the cache is cold while the first requests arrive), each one in turn will acquire the write lock and redo the full manifest load (file read + JSON decode, or an HTTP fetch to the CDN) and overwrite the cache, even though the first one already populated it. true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, including when `readWebAssetsFromFile`/`readWebAssetsFromCDN` returned an error and `result == nil`. In that case a previously successfully cached value is destroyed and the function returns `nil, err`, so every subsequent call must retry the load and callers that don't check the error can get a nil pointer. The assignment should only happen when `err == nil && result != nil`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: `entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally even when the fetch fails, overwriting any previously valid cached value with `nil`.

The file read and the (currently dead, but still reachable) CDN HTTP request at lines 54-67 are executed while the exclusive `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` is held, so all other callers of `GetWebAssets` — including those that would be served from cache in dev mode or during cache refreshes — block on network/disk latency. true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

`d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same bug: passing `name` instead of `options.Kind` when recording metrics, which is inconsistent with other methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive from the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine that does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the *request* context. The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which in practice happens before or right after the goroutine starts. The derived context is therefore already (or immediately) cancelled, so the legacy store call will typically fail with `context canceled` and the legacy database will never be updated. Since mode 3's whole purpose is to keep legacy storage in sync as a safety net, this silently defeats the feature (errors are only recorded in a duration metric, never logged). Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving user/identity values) as the parent before applying the timeout.

Create records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure

In `Create`, when `d.Storage.Create` fails the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. This attributes a unified-storage failure/latency to the legacy backend metric, so the legacy error rate/latency dashboards will show failures that never happened in legacy, and unified-storage create failures are invisible in the storage metric. It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Update records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure

In `Update`, the error branch calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the failure came from `d.Storage.Update`. Same consequence as in `Create`: legacy metrics get polluted with unified-storage failures and storage failures are not counted. Should be `recordStorageDuration`.

Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object already persisted in unified storage

The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` with `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so that legacy storage persisted exactly the object that unified storage had stored. Now the original `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update` from a goroutine. `objInfo.UpdatedObject` will be re-evaluated against legacy's own `old` object, which has a different resourceVersion than unified storage, so for PUT (which carries a resourceVersion) legacy updates can fail with a conflict, and for PATCH/apply the transformers run a second time against a different base producing a different result. The net effect is silent divergence between unified and legacy data – the opposite of what mode 3's legacy mirror is for. Additionally `objInfo`/`obj` are request-scoped values that are now read concurrently after the handler has returned, which is not guaranteed to be safe.

Fire-and-forget goroutines have no panic recovery and no error logging

Each write path launches a bare `go func()` that calls into the legacy store. If the legacy implementation panics (e.g. nil map, nil pointer in a legacy service), the panic is not recovered inside the goroutine and the whole apiserver process crashes – unlike the synchronous path, where the apiserver's handler-level recovery would convert it to a 500. The goroutines also discard the legacy error entirely (only `err != nil` is folded into a histogram label), so operators have no way to find out which objects failed to mirror. Add `defer recover()` with logging and log the legacy error with the object name/kind.

NotFound from unified storage now aborts the legacy delete, leaving orphan legacy rows

The previous mode 3 `Delete` explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. The new code returns early on any storage error, so an object that exists only in legacy (e.g. created before the migration, or whose earlier async legacy mirror failed) can never be deleted from legacy via the API. These orphan rows will resurface if the deployment is ever moved back to a mode that reads from legacy (modes 0–2).

Mode 3 integration tests assert legacy state immediately after k8s writes, which is now asynchronous

The three new mode-3 sub-tests (file line 132, unified line 191, etcd line 287) run `doPlaylistTests`, which after creating playlists through the k8s client immediately queries the legacy endpoint `/api/playlists` and requires the same UIDs (line 523-531), and after each k8s update calls `getFromBothAPIs` comparing legacy DTO fields (line 547). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a detached goroutine with no synchronization, so these assertions race against the background write and the tests will be flaky – and given the cancelled-context problem in the goroutine they are likely to fail deterministically. The tests need to poll/retry the legacy endpoint, or mode 3 must flush legacy writes before responding.

If two threads hit `ensure_loaded!` while the ivar is still nil, both create their own array and one assignment is lost, so the record of already-loaded locales can be dropped and translation files are re-parsed (and the `include?` guard in `translate` can be defeated). The loading of the fallback chain should happen inside `load_locale`/`translate` (or `ensure_loaded!` should be invoked from a single central place), not in a controller filter.

The cache key is `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. With the new fallbacks, the value returned for a given key/locale also depends on `SiteSetting.default_locale` (the second entry of `FallbackLocaleList#[]`). When an admin changes the `default_locale` site setting, previously cached entries that were resolved through the old fallback locale remain in the LRU cache and keep being served for the lifetime of the process (nothing calls `I18n.reload!` on that setting change). Either include the resolved fallback chain in the cache key or clear `@cache` when `default_locale` changes.

`FallbackLocaleList` subclasses `Hash` but overrides `#[]` to always recompute, so every call from `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks#translate` (which happens on *every* translation lookup, not just misses) performs a `SiteSetting.default_locale` read, a `to_sym`, and allocates two arrays (`uniq`, `compact`). Translation lookups with interpolation arguments bypass the LRU cache in translate_accelerator, so this runs on a hot path. Since the class is already a Hash, the computed chain should be memoized per locale and invalidated when `default_locale` changes.

`SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym` raises if the setting is nil, and `uniq` before `compact` cannot protect it

`[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact` calls `to_sym` on the setting value before any nil handling; if `SiteSetting.default_locale` is ever nil/blank (e.g. during early boot, or a site with a cleared setting) this raises `NoMethodError` from inside every translation lookup, which would surface as a 500 on all pages. Note also that `FallbackLocaleList` is defined in an initializer, so it is neither autoloaded nor reloadable, which makes it hard to unit test.

`Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` runs the complete RSS/Atom poll synchronously (HTTP fetch of the feed plus creation/revision of a topic for every item) inside the `retrieve_topic` job each time an unknown embed_url is requested and feed polling is enabled. The behaviour this PR actually changes — several shards being flushed by one worker, and all shards being covered by the shard->process mapping — is untested. `_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere (restarts go through `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)`). Dead code that duplicates restart logic is a maintenance hazard — a future caller would restart a whole process group from a single shard id. Remove it.

The docstring says "Creates one process per shard for parallel processing", but the number of processes is `min(max_processes, len(assigned_shards))`, and the consumer CLI defaults `--flusher-processes` to 1, so the normal configuration is a single process handling all shards. The docstring also still documents `:param topic:` which is not an argument, and does not document the new `max_processes` argument. This misleads operators about the default parallelism.

A new SpansBuffer (and its Redis clients) is created in the parent on every restart without releasing the old one

The parent process keeps using these buffers for `record_stored_segments()` and `get_memory_info()`, so each unhealthy-process restart (up to MAX_PROCESS_RESTARTS per process) leaves the previous buffer's Redis connections unclosed in the parent. y` sanitized to `x
y` gives start=5, end=5, so `sanitized.substring(5, 1)` throws. Instead of a readable "Illegal HTML in key ..." message the plugin crashes with an unrelated runtime exception, hiding the actual problem. Clamp `end` to `min(len) - start` before building the substrings.

`loginTotpStep1=Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:` is Italian text in the Lithuanian login messages. It replaces the former Lithuanian sentence, so the OTP setup screen for the `lt` locale now shows Italian.

All four tests only assert that a violation is reported. New abstract getShortcut() breaks existing OAuth2GrantTypeFactory implementations

`getShortcut()` is added as an abstract method on the `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory` SPI interface. Any third-party/custom grant type factory compiled against a previous release no longer satisfies the interface and will fail with `AbstractMethodError` (or not compile) once deployed - and because `DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit()` iterates all grant factories and calls `getShortcut()`, the failure happens at server start. Providing a `default` implementation (e.g. deriving a shortcut or returning null and handling it) would keep the SPI backwards compatible.

Removal of Context copy constructor is a breaking change

The `public Context(Context context)` copy constructor was deleted from `OAuth2GrantType.Context`. Subclasses outside this repository (and any code that wrapped a Context, e.g. token-exchange contexts) use it; after this change they can no longer compile/link, and there is no replacement that copies an existing Context. If the copy semantics are no longer needed internally, the constructor should still be kept (deprecated) or an equivalent copy path provided.

Context constructor now NPEs on null formParams

The constructor now dereferences `formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`. Previously `formParams` was only stored, so a null value was tolerated by this constructor. Any caller constructing a Context without form parameters now gets a NullPointerException at construction time instead of later (or never). A null-guard (`formParams == null ? null : formParams.getFirst(...)`) would preserve the previous contract.

Decoding throws IllegalArgumentException for any token id containing ':' in an unexpected format

`getTokenContextFromTokenId` treats any id containing ':' as encoded and then throws `IllegalArgumentException` if the prefix is not exactly 6 characters or if a shortcut is unknown. Token ids produced by a different/older encoder, by a custom `TokenContextEncoderProvider`, or by a federated/externally issued token could legitimately contain ':' and would cause an unhandled runtime exception (HTTP 500) in whatever endpoint decodes the id, instead of degrading to an UNKNOWN context like the no-colon case does. Also the message "Expected length of 6" refers to the prefix, not the token id that is printed, which is confusing.

`getShortcutByGrantType`/`getGrantTypeByShortcut` lazily insert into the `ConcurrentHashMap`s for grant types discovered after `postInit`. If a (custom) `OAuth2GrantTypeFactory.getShortcut()` returns null, `grantsByShortcuts.put(null, grantType)` throws NullPointerException; the same happens in `postInit`, failing server startup with an opaque error instead of a message naming the offending factory. In addition, the duplicate-shortcut consistency check performed in `postInit` is not applied on these lazy inserts, so a newly deployed grant with a colliding shortcut silently overwrites an existing mapping, making decoded grant types wrong.

Session type derived from clientSession.getUserSession() instead of the user session already available

`getTokenContextFromClientSessionContext` resolves the user session via `clientSessionContext.getClientSession().getUserSession()` and immediately dereferences it. `TokenManager.initToken`, the only caller, already has a non-null `userSession` parameter it uses for exactly the same persistence-state check. Relying parties, log pipelines and tests that assume `jti` is a UUID (or validate its length/charset) will break. The PR contains no upgrading-guide/release-note entry describing this behaviour change or the new `tokenContextEncoder` SPI.

Any existing consumer that hardcodes 4 as "recreate upgrade needed" – including automation pipelines and any operator/job code that inspects the terminated container's exit code – will now silently interpret "the rolling-updates feature is disabled" as "perform a recreate upgrade", and will no longer recognise a real recreate result (3). Test replaces instead of appending the CR's enabled features

`setEnabledFeatures(List.of(Profile.Feature.ROLLING_UPDATES.getKey()))` unconditionally overwrites whatever `spec.features.enabled` the base test deployment provides. If the shared test CR template ever enables another feature, it is silently dropped here and the test would exercise a different configuration than intended (or fail for an unrelated reason). The existing list should be read and extended with `rolling-updates`.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.

Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate index builds for the same key

BuildIndex previously held `b.cacheMu` for the whole function, which serialized builds and guaranteed that only one index per NamespacedResource was ever constructed. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. Nothing prevents two goroutines from calling BuildIndex for the same key concurrently (e.g. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does an unsynchronized GetIndex-then-build, and it is reachable from both the watch-event handler and concurrent Search calls). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, so the second call fails with a 'path already exists' error and the request errors out; (2) duplicated full index builds waste CPU/IO; (3) the loser's bleve index is overwritten in the cache and never closed, leaking file handles/memory. If the goal is finer-grained locking, a per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed rather than no mutual exclusion at all.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing b.cacheMu locking from the entire BuildIndex function to the final cache assignment permits concurrent goroutines to build duplicate expensive indexes for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map under `b.cacheMu` from arbitrary goroutines (index builds triggered by watch events or search requests). Concurrent map read and map write is a fatal, unrecoverable Go runtime error ('concurrent map read and map write') that crashes the process. Previously this was partially masked because BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole duration; with the finer locking, writes happen far more often and at unpredictable times. TotalDocs should take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unsynchronized iteration of b.cache in TotalDocs racing with concurrent BuildIndex writes, including those triggered by watch events, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

Inside `group.Go(...)` the code does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigning to the `err` declared in the enclosing function, and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed`. With `initWorkers > 1` these are concurrent unsynchronized writes: a genuine data race (will be flagged by `-race`) and, worse, one goroutine's error can be clobbered by another goroutine before `group.Wait()` returns, and `err = group.Wait()` can be overwritten by a still-running assignment. Since this function now runs at server construction and its error aborts startup, misreporting matters. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic counter.

Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the server context and background goroutines

`NewResourceServer` creates `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` and stores `cancel` on the server. When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, the function returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during Init — the storage backend's watch poller started by `searchSupport.init` via `WatchWriteEvents`, and the broadcaster/watcher if `initWatcher` partially succeeded — keeps running against a context that is never cancelled, leaking goroutines, DB connections and the context itself for the lifetime of the process. Call `cancel()` (or `s.Stop`) on the error path.

`Stop` communicates shutdown by setting `s.initErr = "service is stopping"` / `"service is stopped"`, and the only thing that ever read `initErr` on the request path were the `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil` guards that this PR deleted from Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/History/Origin/IsHealthy/PutBlob/GetBlob. After this change, requests arriving after `Stop()` no longer fail fast; they fall through to a backend whose context has been cancelled, producing confusing 'context canceled' errors (or, for blob/diagnostics paths, operating on torn-down state) instead of the intended shutdown error. Either keep a cheap state check at the entry of the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` shutdown signalling in `Stop`.

Index build now runs synchronously in the constructor with an uncancellable, unbounded context

`s.Init(ctx)` is invoked from `NewResourceServer` with a `context.Background()`-derived context that has no deadline, and it performs the full search index build (`searchSupport.init`, which lists every resource of every namespace). Constructing the resource server therefore blocks Grafana/storage-server startup for as long as indexing takes, with no timeout and no way for the caller to cancel; a slow or unresponsive database makes startup hang indefinitely rather than failing or degrading. Consider a bounded context or kicking the index build off asynchronously while keeping the lifecycle/backend init synchronous.

false_positives.candidate:
Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close and then reused after rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, but the per-assignment strategy's `close()`/`terminate()`/`join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the worker threads. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on every partition revocation (rebalance), and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again for the new assignment. On that second call `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes, so a strategy is built around a pool whose worker threads are dead and whose queues are shut down: every `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` swallows in its generic `except Exception` handler and then marks the offset as completed. The consumer will therefore silently drop all messages while still committing their offsets after any rebalance. The pool must be created per assignment (or re-created in `create_with_partitions`) rather than shared across strategy lifetimes.

Unbounded queues mean no backpressure, contradicting the documented guarantee

Each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `arroyo.processing.strategies.abstract.MessageRejected`. As a result the strategy accepts messages from the Kafka consumer as fast as they arrive regardless of worker progress: work items (which also retain the full `Message`/`KafkaPayload`) and their tracked offsets accumulate in memory without bound when a group's processing is slow, which is exactly the scenario this PR is meant to address. This also contradicts the class docstring ("Natural backpressure when queues fill up"). A bounded queue plus `MessageRejected` on `queue.Full` is needed for arroyo to actually throttle consumption.

close() stops the commit thread before draining queues, losing committable offsets

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, and only then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which drains the remaining queued items (`shutdown(immediate=False)` lets queued work finish). Any item processed during that drain completes its offset after the only thread that commits offsets has already exited, so those offsets are never committed. On restart/rebalance all of that work is reprocessed. Additionally `join(timeout)` ignores the supplied timeout and just calls `close()`, so arroyo's shutdown deadline is not honoured. The order should be: stop accepting work, drain the queues, perform a final `get_committable_offsets()` + commit, then stop the commit thread.

Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`commit_offsets` (passed as `commit_function`) is called from `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the arroyo `StreamProcessor` concurrently polls and commits on the main thread. The `Commit` callable given to `create_with_partitions` stages/commits offsets on the shared consumer state and is expected to be called from the processing (main) thread; calling it concurrently races with the processor's own offset staging/commit and with partition revocation (where it can raise `ConsumerError` for unassigned partitions, silently swallowed by the loop's `except Exception`). This can produce lost or incorrect offset commits. Offsets should be collected by the background workers and committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the main thread instead.

A single missing offset permanently blocks all commits for the partition

`get_committable_offsets()` walks offsets contiguously from `last_committed + 1` and `break`s on the first offset that is not present in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous as seen by a consumer (transactional/control records, compaction, or any message that never reaches `submit` because an upstream wrapper such as the DLQ/stale-message wrapper consumed it). If one offset in the sequence is never added, that partition can never advance its commit point: `all_offsets` grows without bound and the consumer group lag never decreases, causing full reprocessing of everything after the gap on restart. There needs to be a mechanism to advance past offsets that will never be seen (e.g. seed the committed position from the assignment and treat unknown offsets below the current max as done).

Generic exception handler in submit() drops messages and commits their offsets

`submit()` wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one `try/except Exception`; on any failure (including a failing `grouping_fn`, a `FilteredPayload` payload which trips the `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` in `decode_payload`, or `queue.ShutDown` from a shut-down pool) it logs and then marks the offset as both added and completed. The message is silently discarded and its offset is committed, so the data is lost with no DLQ and no visible failure other than a log line. Expected non-processable cases (filtered payloads, decode failures) should be handled explicitly, and unexpected enqueue failures should either raise (so arroyo can DLQ/stop) rather than ack the offset.

Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys hash into exactly all 3 queues (`len(queue_indices) == 3`). `get_queue_for_group` uses `hash()` on a `str`, which is salted per interpreter run (PYTHONHASHSEED), so there is a small but non-zero chance (~0.1%) that one bucket receives no key and the test fails for unrelated reasons. Assert something weaker (e.g. `len(queue_indices) > 1`) or use a deterministic hash function.

Per-worker queue-depth gauge is emitted with identical tags from all workers

Every `OrderedQueueWorker` emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` with only an `identifier` tag, so all N workers (20 by default) report the depth of their own queue under the same metric series. The values overwrite each other and the resulting gauge is meaningless for diagnosing a backed-up individual queue — which is the main failure mode this design is meant to surface. Add a `worker_id`/queue index tag or emit the max/aggregate from one place.

Worker transaction name hardcodes the "monitors" prefix

The sentry transaction created per work item is named `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this strategy is generic to remote subscriptions and is being enabled for the uptime consumer. Transactions for uptime results will be grouped under a `monitors.` namespace, making performance data misleading/hard to find.

`zunionstore` is called without `AGGREGATE`, so Redis sums the scores of members present in both source zsets. Since the score is `end_timestamp_precise` and used for eviction ordering (`zpopmin`), any span payload that exists in both the span's own set and the target set (e.g. a re-delivered/duplicated span, which the comments elsewhere acknowledge can happen when partitioning assumptions break) gets a score of roughly twice the timestamp. That span then sorts as the newest and is retained while genuinely newer spans are evicted. Use `AGGREGATE MIN` (or MAX) to keep scores meaningful.

The previous code emitted `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and logged an error when a segment exceeded the span-count limit. Segments silently lose spans in production with no way to detect or quantify the data loss. Add a counter/metric for evicted spans (e.g. return the evicted count from the Lua script and record it).

The redirect-resolution loop bound was changed from `0, 10000` to `0, 1000` and the comment documenting the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. This is an unrelated, undocumented behaviour change: segment trees deeper than 1000 redirects will now be split into multiple segments instead of being joined. Either restore the previous bound or keep the comment and justify the new value.

The headline change of this PR is eviction during insert (set -> sorted set, `zpopmin` when a segment exceeds 1000 spans), but no test exercises a segment larger than the cap, verifies which spans are kept (newest by `end_timestamp_precise`), or verifies that scores survive the `zunionstore` merge path. The module docstring (steps 3 and the glossary line "span-buf:s:* -- the actual set keys") still says spans are added to a Redis set, but the implementation now uses sorted sets keyed by `end_timestamp_precise`, and segments are capped at 1000 spans with the oldest evicted during insert. `val["end_timestamp_precise"]` is read with a hard subscript while every other field that may be absent uses `.get()`. If any message on `ingest-spans` lacks the field (older producer, replayed backlog, malformed payload) this raises `KeyError` inside `process_batch`, which fails the whole batch and puts the consumer into a crash loop rather than dropping or defaulting the single message. Authenticated GitHub user is not verified when the Integration row does not yet exist

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch`, if `Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id)` raises `DoesNotExist` the pipeline advances immediately (`return pipeline.next_step()`) without any comparison of `github_authenticated_user` against the account that installed the app. The sender information this check relies on is written by the asynchronous `installation` webhook, so whether the validation runs at all depends on webhook delivery timing: an attacker who knows a victim's `installation_id` and completes the redirect before the webhook is processed bypasses the new check entirely. Pass already-lazy/translated values from the call sites instead of translating the variable.

Login-cache invalidation on update is decided from the organization-aware wrapper, so it depends on transient organization state

`update()` passes `idpById` (obtained from `getById()`, which returns the anonymous `IdentityProviderModel` subclass created by `createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel`) into `registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate`. That wrapper's `isEnabled()` returns `false` whenever the linked organization (or the organization provider for the realm) is disabled, even though the stored IDP row is enabled. As a result `getLoginPredicate().test(original)` can evaluate to `false` for an IDP that *is* present in the cached login ID sets (the DB query behind `getForLogin` only filters on the IDP's own `enabled` flag, not on the organization state). In that situation an update that really removes the IDP from the login set (e.g. setting `hideOnLogin=true` or clearing `kc.org.broker.public`) takes the `!test(original) && !test(updated)` early return and does *not* invalidate `*.idp.login.*`. Because enabling/disabling an organization (a group attribute change) also does not invalidate those keys, after the organization is re-enabled `getForLogin` keeps returning the now hidden/non-public provider - `getForLogin` never re-applies the login predicate to the re-resolved models, and callers only re-check `isEnabled()`. Note the inconsistency with `remove()`, which correctly uses the unwrapped `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)`; `update()` should likewise use the raw stored model (or compare only the IDP's own fields).

New invalidation paths in create()/remove() are only tested for the negative case

The test only removes `idp-alias-1` (a disabled provider, i.e. not login-eligible) and only creates `idp-alias-20` with `hideOnLogin=true`, so both assertions verify that the login caches are *not* invalidated. The newly added `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(model)` in `create()` and `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(storedIdp)` in `remove()` are therefore never exercised in their positive branch: a regression that drops either call (leaving the login caches stale after adding or deleting a login-eligible broker) would not be caught. Add a case that creates an enabled, non-hidden provider and one that removes a login-eligible provider, and assert the `*.idp.login.*` entries disappear.

The search key is always derived from `organizationId`, but for `FetchMode.REALM_ONLY` the delegate ignores `organizationId` entirely (it forces `ORGANIZATION_ID=null`). Any caller invoking `getForLogin(REALM_ONLY, someOrgId)` therefore creates a distinct search key for a logically identical result, and each new key triggers `cache.invalidateObject(cacheKey)` plus a full re-query before being merged back. For `ORG_ONLY`/`ALL`, one cached `IdentityProviderListQuery` per realm accumulates one entry per organization id ever queried, with no bound or pruning, so memory grows with the number of organizations that are used for login. Consider using an empty search key for REALM_ONLY and bounding/keying per-organization results separately.

The cached implementation collects internal ids into a `HashSet` and returns `new HashSet<>(...).stream()`, so the order of the returned providers is unspecified and can differ between calls/JVMs. Before this change the stream order followed the underlying query order (realm-level providers first, then organization providers, in the order produced by JPA). true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

After the fast path with the read lock fails, the function takes the write lock but never re-reads `entryPointAssetsCache`. If N goroutines reach this point concurrently at startup (the common case, since the cache is cold while the first requests arrive), each one in turn will acquire the write lock and redo the full manifest load (file read + JSON decode, or an HTTP fetch to the CDN) and overwrite the cache, even though the first one already populated it. Re-checking `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after `Lock()` removes this thundering-herd work.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
A failed load overwrites a previously valid cache with nil

`entryPointAssetsCache = result` is executed unconditionally, including when `readWebAssetsFromFile`/`readWebAssetsFromCDN` returned an error and `result == nil`. In that case a previously successfully cached value is destroyed and the function returns `nil, err`, so every subsequent call must retry the load and callers that don't check the error can get a nil pointer. The assignment should only happen when `err == nil && result != nil`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the unconditional assignment of the fetch result to entryPointAssetsCache, which overwrites a previously valid cache with nil when fetching fails.

false_positives.candidate:

The file read and the (currently dead, but still reachable) CDN HTTP request at lines 54-67 are executed while the exclusive `entryPointAssetsCacheMu.Lock()` is held, so all other callers of `GetWebAssets` — including those that would be served from cache in dev mode or during cache refreshes — block on network/disk latency. Loading outside the lock and only taking the write lock to publish the result would avoid serializing request handling on I/O.

The PR fixes a data race on the `entryPointAssetsCache` global but adds no test. A simple test that calls `GetWebAssets` from multiple goroutines (which fails under `-race` before the fix) would prevent the race from being reintroduced, e.g. by a future refactor that drops the mutex.

Each iteration reallocates and copies the whole accumulated string, so for a batch of ~32k IDs (the size exercised by the new test) this performs ~32k allocations and copies of an ever-growing ~200KB string, i.e. gigabytes of memcpy per batch, repeated for every batch of the cleanup loop. `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's `name` where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. Because `name` is a per-object identifier, each deleted resource creates a new Prometheus time series on the storage duration histogram, leading to unbounded cardinality and potential memory blow-up in both Grafana and the scraping Prometheus. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same incorrect metrics argument: Delete passes the object's name instead of options.Kind, unlike other methods. The candidate adds cardinality consequences but describes the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive from the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine that does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the *request* context. The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which in practice happens before or right after the goroutine starts. The derived context is therefore already (or immediately) cancelled, so the legacy store call will typically fail with `context canceled` and the legacy database will never be updated. Since mode 3's whole purpose is to keep legacy storage in sync as a safety net, this silently defeats the feature (errors are only recorded in a duration metric, never logged). Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving user/identity values) as the parent before applying the timeout.

Create records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure

In `Create`, when `d.Storage.Create` fails the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. This attributes a unified-storage failure/latency to the legacy backend metric, so the legacy error rate/latency dashboards will show failures that never happened in legacy, and unified-storage create failures are invisible in the storage metric. It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Update records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure

In `Update`, the error branch calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the failure came from `d.Storage.Update`. Same consequence as in `Create`: legacy metrics get polluted with unified-storage failures and storage failures are not counted. Should be `recordStorageDuration`.

DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records a storage duration instead of a legacy duration

Inside the background goroutine of `DeleteCollection`, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` with `startLegacy`. This reports legacy latency/errors under the unified-storage metric, double counting storage observations for delete-collection and leaving legacy delete-collection completely unmeasured. Should be `recordLegacyDuration`.

Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object already persisted in unified storage

The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` with `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so that legacy storage persisted exactly the object that unified storage had stored. Now the original `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update` from a goroutine. `objInfo.UpdatedObject` will be re-evaluated against legacy's own `old` object, which has a different resourceVersion than unified storage, so for PUT (which carries a resourceVersion) legacy updates can fail with a conflict, and for PATCH/apply the transformers run a second time against a different base producing a different result. The net effect is silent divergence between unified and legacy data – the opposite of what mode 3's legacy mirror is for. Additionally `objInfo`/`obj` are request-scoped values that are now read concurrently after the handler has returned, which is not guaranteed to be safe.

Fire-and-forget goroutines have no panic recovery and no error logging

Each write path launches a bare `go func()` that calls into the legacy store. If the legacy implementation panics (e.g. nil map, nil pointer in a legacy service), the panic is not recovered inside the goroutine and the whole apiserver process crashes – unlike the synchronous path, where the apiserver's handler-level recovery would convert it to a 500. The goroutines also discard the legacy error entirely (only `err != nil` is folded into a histogram label), so operators have no way to find out which objects failed to mirror. Add `defer recover()` with logging and log the legacy error with the object name/kind.

NotFound from unified storage now aborts the legacy delete, leaving orphan legacy rows

The previous mode 3 `Delete` explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. The new code returns early on any storage error, so an object that exists only in legacy (e.g. created before the migration, or whose earlier async legacy mirror failed) can never be deleted from legacy via the API. These orphan rows will resurface if the deployment is ever moved back to a mode that reads from legacy (modes 0–2).

Mode 3 integration tests assert legacy state immediately after k8s writes, which is now asynchronous

The three new mode-3 sub-tests (file line 132, unified line 191, etcd line 287) run `doPlaylistTests`, which after creating playlists through the k8s client immediately queries the legacy endpoint `/api/playlists` and requires the same UIDs (line 523-531), and after each k8s update calls `getFromBothAPIs` comparing legacy DTO fields (line 547). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a detached goroutine with no synchronization, so these assertions race against the background write and the tests will be flaky – and given the cancelled-context problem in the goroutine they are likely to fail deterministically. The tests need to poll/retry the legacy endpoint, or mode 3 must flush legacy writes before responding.

Unit tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy write

All mode-3 write tests (`Create`, `Delete`, `Update`, `DeleteCollection`) assert only on the value returned from unified storage and return immediately; nothing calls `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` or waits for the goroutine that performs the legacy write. The central new behaviour of mode 3 – that legacy is also written – is therefore completely untested (the cancelled-context bug above would not be caught). Worse, the goroutine may invoke the shared `mock.Mock` after the sub-test has finished; if the arguments don't match a registered expectation testify panics from that goroutine and takes down the whole test binary. Add a synchronization point (e.g. a channel closed from the mock's Run function) and assert the legacy call happened with the expected arguments.

Migration crashes when the `embed_category` site setting row does not exist

The migration does `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories AS c INNER JOIN site_settings AS s ON s.value = c.name WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id']`. `embed_category` defaulted to '' and is only persisted in `site_settings` if an admin changed it, so on the vast majority of installs this query returns zero rows and `result[0]` is nil/out of range, raising before the data migration can run. The whole `rake db:migrate` then fails and the deploy is blocked. The row lookup needs to be guarded (e.g. fetch into a variable and check for presence) before dereferencing.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same unchecked dereference of execute(...)[0]['id'], which crashes when the embed_category query returns no rows. The candidate's deployment-impact description does not change the underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback query also dereferences a possibly-missing site_settings row

`execute("SELECT value FROM site_settings WHERE name = 'uncategorized_category_id'")[0]['value']` assumes the `uncategorized_category_id` setting is stored in the database. It is a hidden setting with default -1 and is frequently absent from `site_settings`, so this raises in the same way as the `embed_category` lookup. Even when present it can be -1, which would be inserted into `embeddable_hosts.category_id` (declared NOT NULL but with no FK), producing rows that point at a non-existent category.

`create_table ... force: true` can silently drop an existing table

`force: true` issues a DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating `embeddable_hosts`. If the migration is ever re-run, or if a table with that name already exists (e.g. created by a plugin or a partially applied migration), all existing embeddable host configuration is destroyed without warning. `force: true` should not be used in a schema migration.

No index or uniqueness constraint on embeddable_hosts.host

`EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` runs `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` on every `embed/comments` and `embed/count` request as well as in TopicRetriever, but the table has no index on `host` (and `lower(host)` would need a functional index anyway), so every embed request does a sequential scan. There is also no unique index or model-level uniqueness validation, so the admin UI happily creates duplicate rows for the same host, after which `record_for_host` returns an arbitrary one and the "post to category" mapping becomes non-deterministic.

has_many uses `embed: :ids` without `include: true`, so hosts are never sent

With ActiveModel::Serializers `embed: :ids` and no `include: true`, the payload contains only `embeddable_host_ids` and no top-level `embeddable_hosts` collection. The client's `store._hydrateEmbedded` resolves `*_ids` by looking up `root['embeddable_hosts']`; when that collection is absent `_lookupSubType` returns undefined for each id, so `embedding.embeddable_hosts` becomes an array of `undefined` and the admin Embedding page renders empty rows. Either sideload the objects (`embed: :ids, include: true`) or embed objects directly.

`*_ids` hydration crashes on null and silently produces undefined entries

In `_hydrateEmbedded` the new plural branch calls `obj[k].map(...)` without checking that the value is an array, so a serializer sending `"foo_ids": null` throws a TypeError and the whole hydration (and therefore the find/findAll promise) fails. Additionally, when `_lookupSubType` cannot resolve an id (collection not sideloaded) it returns `undefined`, and those `undefined` values are pushed into the resulting array instead of being filtered out; the `hydrated || []` fallback is dead code since `map` always returns an array. Guard for non-array values and compact the results.

PUT /admin/customize/embedding ignores its payload and saves nothing

`update` only re-renders the freshly built OpenStruct; it never reads `params` or persists anything. The matching client code (`admin-embedding.js.es6` `saveChanges` calling `embedding.update({})`) therefore does nothing either. Either implement the update or remove the route/action and the dead `saveChanges` action so callers aren't misled into believing changes were saved.

New write endpoints have no behavioural or authorization tests

The only assertion is that the class inherits from Admin::AdminController. There is no coverage for create/update/destroy (including the uncategorized-category fallback, invalid host validation errors, and missing-id handling, which currently 500s), nor for the fact that non-staff/non-admin users must be rejected from these new state-changing admin routes. Given this PR introduces a new writable admin resource, request specs for success, validation failure and access control are needed.

Test named "is false if embeddable_host is blank" no longer tests that condition

`Topic#expandable_first_post?` no longer consults embeddable hosts at all, so this example passes merely because `embed_truncate` defaults to false and `has_topic_embed?` is false for an unsaved topic. The name is now misleading and the example asserts nothing about hosts; it should be renamed/removed so future readers aren't misled about what behaviour is covered.

Underscore-to-dash conversion only replaces the first underscore

`type.replace('_', '-')` with a string pattern replaces a single occurrence, so a type such as `some_embeddable_host` would become `some-embeddable_host` and fail the ADMIN_MODELS lookup, silently routing the request to the non-admin base path. Use `/_/g` (or `Ember.String.dasherize`) so all underscores are converted.
