`int order();` is added to the public `CryptoProvider` interface without a `default` implementation. `CryptoProvider` is an SPI loaded via `ServiceLoader`, so any implementation outside this repository (adapters, downstream/3rd-party crypto providers, test doubles) will fail to compile and will throw `AbstractMethodError` at runtime when `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` sorts providers. Giving the method a sensible `default` (e.g. `return 100;` or `0`) would keep the SPI backward compatible while still allowing providers to override the preference.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same backward-compatibility break: adding abstract order() to the public CryptoProvider SPI without a default forces existing implementations to change and can fail at runtime.

false_positives.candidate:
Equal-order providers are now silently resolved instead of failing fast (FIPS vs non-FIPS)

The previous code threw `IllegalStateException` when more than one `CryptoProvider` was found, which protected against a misconfigured classpath. Now the list is sorted by `order()` and the first entry is used unconditionally. `DefaultCryptoProvider`, `WildFlyElytronProvider` and `FIPS1402Provider` all return `order() == 200`, so if e.g. both the default (non-FIPS BouncyCastle) and the FIPS provider jars end up on the classpath, the selection depends on undefined `ServiceLoader` iteration order and the server may silently start with the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider in a deployment that must be FIPS-compliant, with only a debug-level log line. Either keep failing on an order tie, or give the server-side providers distinct orders and log at WARN when multiple providers of the same order are present.

Dynamic string passed as format to logger.debugf

`logger.debugf(builder.toString())` passes a dynamically built message as the format string of a formatting logger method (with no arguments). Any `%` character appearing in a provider class name would cause an `UnknownFormatConversionException`/`MissingFormatArgumentException` from the logging call. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` or `logger.debugf("%s", builder)` instead.

concatenatedRSToASN1DER does not validate the input signature length

`System.arraycopy(signature, 0, r, 1, len)` / `System.arraycopy(signature, len, s, 1, len)` assume `signature.length == signLength`. For an attacker-supplied token whose signature part is shorter (or where the wrong algorithm length is used), this throws an unchecked `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` out of a method declared to throw `IOException`, so callers doing signature verification will see an unexpected runtime failure instead of a clean "invalid signature" error. The BouncyCastle-based implementations validate the length and throw `IOException`; the same check should be added here.

The key pair is generated once with `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC")` default parameters (P-256), so the ES384 and ES512 cases are exercised with 32-byte r/s values zero-padded to 48/66 bytes; the real cases (secp384r1/secp521r1 signatures, including the 521-bit odd byte length that is the usual source of off-by-one bugs) are never covered. In addition the test only asserts a round-trip of the new implementation against itself (`rsConcat` vs `rsConcat2`), so a systematic encoding error would pass. The test should generate a key per curve (`ECGenParameterSpec` secp256r1/secp384r1/secp521r1) and verify the DER output with `Signature.verify()` (and/or compare with the BouncyCastle-based provider output).

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator uses integer key semantics but is wired to a datetime-ordered queryset

`OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key` does `math.floor(getattr(item, self.key))` and `value_from_cursor` returns the raw cursor value, i.e. it assumes the sort key is numeric (the `Paginator` semantics). The new audit-log code path instantiates it with `order_by="-datetime"` on `AuditLogEntry`, whose `datetime` field is a `datetime` object. `math.floor(datetime)` raises `TypeError`, and `build_queryset` would compare the datetime column against a raw integer cursor value in the generated `WHERE ... <= %s` clause, producing a database error. The optimized path therefore cannot work for this endpoint at all; it needs to derive from `DateTimePaginator` (or convert values) and have tests covering datetime keys.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: get_item_key/paginator assumes a numeric sort key and applies math.floor, but the audit-log path orders by datetime, so a datetime key raises TypeError and cannot be paginated correctly.

false_positives.candidate:
Advanced pagination gated on has_global_access / non-elevated is_superuser

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` is described as enabling the feature for "authorized administrators", but `has_global_access` merely means the member has access to all teams (it is true for every member in an organization with open membership), so any ordinary org member can turn on the unbounded/negative-offset pagination path. In addition, `request.user.is_superuser` is the raw staff flag; Sentry requires the active-superuser check (`is_active_superuser(request)`) so that superuser privileges are only honored when the superuser session is elevated. Both checks should be replaced with a proper permission/feature check.

Offset clamping in BasePaginator is inconsistent and leaves invalid cursors in the response

`start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` silently clamps negative offsets only for forward cursors; a previous-page cursor with a negative offset is still passed straight into the queryset slice and will raise `ValueError: Negative indexing is not supported.` from Django. For the clamped forward case the negative `cursor.offset` is still handed to `build_cursor`, where `_build_next_values` computes `next_offset = offset + limit` from the negative value, so the returned next/prev cursors keep propagating out-of-range offsets. Invalid cursor offsets should be rejected with `BadPaginationError` (400) rather than partially clamped.

Extra-row trim uses raw cursor offset instead of the effective start offset

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` the check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` compares the fetched row count against the raw `cursor.offset`, but the rows were fetched using `start_offset` (which may differ from `offset` after clamping, and is negative in the "advanced" branch). When they diverge the extra look-ahead row is not dropped, so a previous-page response can include a row that belongs to the adjacent page.

New paginator and offset-clamping behavior have no tests

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` and the new offset-clamping logic in `BasePaginator.get_result` change pagination semantics (negative offsets, boundary trimming) but no tests are added. Given the class is dead-on-arrival for datetime keys and crashes on negative offsets, basic unit tests for zero/negative/large offsets and for the audit-log endpoint with `optimized_pagination=true` are needed before merging.

Comment claims negative offsets are supported although nothing validates or supports them

The added comment in `Cursor.__init__` states that negative offsets are allowed as a "performance optimization ... enables efficient reverse pagination". No validation or support was added here, and every consumer (Django queryset slicing, `OffsetPaginator`, `ChainPaginator`) either rejects negative offsets or crashes on them. The comment will mislead future readers into believing negative offsets are a supported contract.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the BuildIndex-wide lock allows concurrent duplicate index builds for the same key

BuildIndex previously held `b.cacheMu` for the whole function, which serialized builds and guaranteed that only one index per NamespacedResource was ever constructed. Now the lock is only taken around the final `b.cache[key] = idx` write. Nothing prevents two goroutines from calling BuildIndex for the same key concurrently (e.g. `searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex` does an unsynchronized GetIndex-then-build, and it is reachable from both the watch-event handler and concurrent Search calls). Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes both goroutines call `bleve.New(dir, ...)` on the same directory, so the second call fails with a 'path already exists' error and the request errors out; (2) duplicated full index builds waste CPU/IO; (3) the loser's bleve index is overwritten in the cache and never closed, leaking file handles/memory. If the goal is finer-grained locking, a per-key lock (or singleflight) is needed rather than no mutual exclusion at all.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same race condition: moving b.cacheMu from protecting the entire BuildIndex function to only the final cache assignment allows concurrent goroutines to build the same index for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu

`TotalDocs` ranges over `b.cache` with no lock while `BuildIndex` now writes to that map under `b.cacheMu` from arbitrary goroutines (index builds triggered by watch events or search requests). Concurrent map read and map write is a fatal, unrecoverable Go runtime error ('concurrent map read and map write') that crashes the process. Previously this was partially masked because BuildIndex held the write lock for its whole duration; with the finer locking, writes happen far more often and at unpredictable times. TotalDocs should take `b.cacheMu.RLock()`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: TotalDocs ranges over b.cache without holding cacheMu while concurrent BuildIndex writes can occur, risking a fatal concurrent map read/write panic. The candidate adds the appropriate RLock fix but describes the same underlying bug.

false_positives.candidate:
errgroup goroutines share the outer `err` and `totalBatchesIndexed` variables (data race, lost errors)

Inside `group.Go(...)` the code does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` assigning to the `err` declared in the enclosing function, and increments the shared `totalBatchesIndexed`. With `initWorkers > 1` these are concurrent unsynchronized writes: a genuine data race (will be flagged by `-race`) and, worse, one goroutine's error can be clobbered by another goroutine before `group.Wait()` returns, and `err = group.Wait()` can be overwritten by a still-running assignment. Since this function now runs at server construction and its error aborts startup, misreporting matters. Use a local `err :=` inside the closure and an atomic counter.

Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks the server context and background goroutines

`NewResourceServer` creates `ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(...)` and stores `cancel` on the server. When `s.Init(ctx)` fails, the function returns `nil, err` without calling `cancel()`. Anything already started during Init — the storage backend's watch poller started by `searchSupport.init` via `WatchWriteEvents`, and the broadcaster/watcher if `initWatcher` partially succeeded — keeps running against a context that is never cancelled, leaking goroutines, DB connections and the context itself for the lifetime of the process. Call `cancel()` (or `s.Stop`) on the error path.

Removing per-request Init() checks means requests are still served after Stop()

`Stop` communicates shutdown by setting `s.initErr = "service is stopping"` / `"service is stopped"`, and the only thing that ever read `initErr` on the request path were the `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil` guards that this PR deleted from Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Watch/Search/History/Origin/IsHealthy/PutBlob/GetBlob. After this change, requests arriving after `Stop()` no longer fail fast; they fall through to a backend whose context has been cancelled, producing confusing 'context canceled' errors (or, for blob/diagnostics paths, operating on torn-down state) instead of the intended shutdown error. Either keep a cheap state check at the entry of the handlers or drop the now-dead `initErr` shutdown signalling in `Stop`.

Index build now runs synchronously in the constructor with an uncancellable, unbounded context

`s.Init(ctx)` is invoked from `NewResourceServer` with a `context.Background()`-derived context that has no deadline, and it performs the full search index build (`searchSupport.init`, which lists every resource of every namespace). Constructing the resource server therefore blocks Grafana/storage-server startup for as long as indexing takes, with no timeout and no way for the caller to cancel; a slow or unresponsive database makes startup hang indefinitely rather than failing or degrading. Consider a bounded context or kicking the index build off asynchronously while keeping the lifecycle/backend init synchronous.

Storage-server integration test now skipped for postgres, leaving only mysql coverage

With sqlite3 already skipped, adding an unconditional skip for postgres means `TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer` only ever runs against mysql in CI. Given this PR changes resource-server startup to initialize unified storage (including index building) inside `NewResourceServer`, the postgres startup path is exactly what this test would have covered. The TODO has no tracking issue; at minimum reference one so the coverage gap is not forgotten.

false_positives.candidate:
Queue pool is destroyed on strategy close and then reused after rebalance

`FixedQueuePool` is created once in `ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__`, but the per-assignment strategy's `close()`/`terminate()`/`join()` call `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which sets `worker.shutdown = True`, calls `queue.shutdown()` on every queue and joins the worker threads. Arroyo calls `close()`/`join()` on every partition revocation (rebalance), and then calls `create_with_partitions()` again for the new assignment. On that second call `assert self.queue_pool is not None` still passes, so a strategy is built around a pool whose worker threads are dead and whose queues are shut down: every `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`, which `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit` swallows in its generic `except Exception` handler and then marks the offset as completed. The consumer will therefore silently drop all messages while still committing their offsets after any rebalance. The pool must be created per assignment (or re-created in `create_with_partitions`) rather than shared across strategy lifetimes.

Unbounded queues mean no backpressure, contradicting the documented guarantee

Each queue is created as `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize`, and `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit()` never raises `arroyo.processing.strategies.abstract.MessageRejected`. As a result the strategy accepts messages from the Kafka consumer as fast as they arrive regardless of worker progress: work items (which also retain the full `Message`/`KafkaPayload`) and their tracked offsets accumulate in memory without bound when a group's processing is slow, which is exactly the scenario this PR is meant to address. This also contradicts the class docstring ("Natural backpressure when queues fill up"). A bounded queue plus `MessageRejected` on `queue.Full` is needed for arroyo to actually throttle consumption.

close() stops the commit thread before draining queues, losing committable offsets

`close()` sets `shutdown_event`, joins the commit thread, and only then calls `queue_pool.shutdown()`, which drains the remaining queued items (`shutdown(immediate=False)` lets queued work finish). Any item processed during that drain completes its offset after the only thread that commits offsets has already exited, so those offsets are never committed. On restart/rebalance all of that work is reprocessed. Additionally `join(timeout)` ignores the supplied timeout and just calls `close()`, so arroyo's shutdown deadline is not honoured. The order should be: stop accepting work, drain the queues, perform a final `get_committable_offsets()` + commit, then stop the commit thread.

Arroyo commit callback is invoked from a background thread

`commit_offsets` (passed as `commit_function`) is called from `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`, a separate daemon thread, while the arroyo `StreamProcessor` concurrently polls and commits on the main thread. The `Commit` callable given to `create_with_partitions` stages/commits offsets on the shared consumer state and is expected to be called from the processing (main) thread; calling it concurrently races with the processor's own offset staging/commit and with partition revocation (where it can raise `ConsumerError` for unassigned partitions, silently swallowed by the loop's `except Exception`). This can produce lost or incorrect offset commits. Offsets should be collected by the background workers and committed from `poll()`/`submit()` on the main thread instead.

A single missing offset permanently blocks all commits for the partition

`get_committable_offsets()` walks offsets contiguously from `last_committed + 1` and `break`s on the first offset that is not present in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not guaranteed to be contiguous as seen by a consumer (transactional/control records, compaction, or any message that never reaches `submit` because an upstream wrapper such as the DLQ/stale-message wrapper consumed it). If one offset in the sequence is never added, that partition can never advance its commit point: `all_offsets` grows without bound and the consumer group lag never decreases, causing full reprocessing of everything after the gap on restart. There needs to be a mechanism to advance past offsets that will never be seen (e.g. seed the committed position from the assignment and treat unknown offsets below the current max as done).

Generic exception handler in submit() drops messages and commits their offsets

`submit()` wraps decoding, grouping and enqueueing in one `try/except Exception`; on any failure (including a failing `grouping_fn`, a `FilteredPayload` payload which trips the `assert not isinstance(payload, FilteredPayload)` in `decode_payload`, or `queue.ShutDown` from a shut-down pool) it logs and then marks the offset as both added and completed. The message is silently discarded and its offset is committed, so the data is lost with no DLQ and no visible failure other than a log line. Expected non-processable cases (filtered payloads, decode failures) should be handled explicitly, and unexpected enqueue failures should either raise (so arroyo can DLQ/stop) rather than ack the offset.

Distribution test depends on randomized string hashing

`test_different_groups_distributed` asserts that 20 group keys hash into exactly all 3 queues (`len(queue_indices) == 3`). `get_queue_for_group` uses `hash()` on a `str`, which is salted per interpreter run (PYTHONHASHSEED), so there is a small but non-zero chance (~0.1%) that one bucket receives no key and the test fails for unrelated reasons. Assert something weaker (e.g. `len(queue_indices) > 1`) or use a deterministic hash function.

Per-worker queue-depth gauge is emitted with identical tags from all workers

Every `OrderedQueueWorker` emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` with only an `identifier` tag, so all N workers (20 by default) report the depth of their own queue under the same metric series. The values overwrite each other and the resulting gauge is meaningless for diagnosing a backed-up individual queue — which is the main failure mode this design is meant to surface. Add a `worker_id`/queue index tag or emit the max/aggregate from one place.

Worker transaction name hardcodes the "monitors" prefix

The sentry transaction created per work item is named `f"monitors.{self.identifier}.worker_{self.worker_id}"`, but this strategy is generic to remote subscriptions and is being enabled for the uptime consumer. Transactions for uptime results will be grouped under a `monitors.` namespace, making performance data misleading/hard to find.

In that case a previously successfully cached value is destroyed and the function returns `nil, err`, so every subsequent call must retry the load and callers that don't check the error can get a nil pointer. The assignment should only happen when `err == nil && result != nil`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.

Because `name` is a per-object identifier, each deleted resource creates a new Prometheus time series on the storage duration histogram, leading to unbounded cardinality and potential memory blow-up in both Grafana and the scraping Prometheus. true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: Delete passes the object name instead of options.Kind to recordStorageDuration, unlike other call sites. The candidate correctly flags the inconsistency and its metric-cardinality impact.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive from the request context, which is cancelled when the handler returns

All four write paths (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) spawn a goroutine that does `context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, ...)` using the *request* context. The apiserver cancels the request context as soon as the HTTP handler returns, which in practice happens before or right after the goroutine starts. The derived context is therefore already (or immediately) cancelled, so the legacy store call will typically fail with `context canceled` and the legacy database will never be updated. Since mode 3's whole purpose is to keep legacy storage in sync as a safety net, this silently defeats the feature (errors are only recorded in a duration metric, never logged). Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (preserving user/identity values) as the parent before applying the timeout.

Create records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure

In `Create`, when `d.Storage.Create` fails the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...)` with `startStorage`. This attributes a unified-storage failure/latency to the legacy backend metric, so the legacy error rate/latency dashboards will show failures that never happened in legacy, and unified-storage create failures are invisible in the storage metric. It should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`.

Update records a legacy-storage duration on a unified-storage failure

In `Update`, the error branch calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the failure came from `d.Storage.Update`. Same consequence as in `Create`: legacy metrics get polluted with unified-storage failures and storage failures are not counted. Should be `recordStorageDuration`.

DeleteCollection's legacy goroutine records a storage duration instead of a legacy duration

Inside the background goroutine of `DeleteCollection`, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded via `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...)` with `startLegacy`. This reports legacy latency/errors under the unified-storage metric, double counting storage observations for delete-collection and leaving legacy delete-collection completely unmeasured. Should be `recordLegacyDuration`.

Legacy Update is given the raw objInfo instead of the object already persisted in unified storage

The previous implementation wrapped `objInfo` with `&updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: obj}` so that legacy storage persisted exactly the object that unified storage had stored. Now the original `objInfo` is handed to `d.Legacy.Update` from a goroutine. `objInfo.UpdatedObject` will be re-evaluated against legacy's own `old` object, which has a different resourceVersion than unified storage, so for PUT (which carries a resourceVersion) legacy updates can fail with a conflict, and for PATCH/apply the transformers run a second time against a different base producing a different result. The net effect is silent divergence between unified and legacy data – the opposite of what mode 3's legacy mirror is for. Additionally `objInfo`/`obj` are request-scoped values that are now read concurrently after the handler has returned, which is not guaranteed to be safe.

Fire-and-forget goroutines have no panic recovery and no error logging

Each write path launches a bare `go func()` that calls into the legacy store. If the legacy implementation panics (e.g. nil map, nil pointer in a legacy service), the panic is not recovered inside the goroutine and the whole apiserver process crashes – unlike the synchronous path, where the apiserver's handler-level recovery would convert it to a 500. The goroutines also discard the legacy error entirely (only `err != nil` is folded into a histogram label), so operators have no way to find out which objects failed to mirror. Add `defer recover()` with logging and log the legacy error with the object name/kind.

NotFound from unified storage now aborts the legacy delete, leaving orphan legacy rows

The previous mode 3 `Delete` explicitly tolerated `apierrors.IsNotFound` from unified storage and still attempted the legacy delete. The new code returns early on any storage error, so an object that exists only in legacy (e.g. created before the migration, or whose earlier async legacy mirror failed) can never be deleted from legacy via the API. These orphan rows will resurface if the deployment is ever moved back to a mode that reads from legacy (modes 0–2).

Mode 3 integration tests assert legacy state immediately after k8s writes, which is now asynchronous

The three new mode-3 sub-tests (file line 132, unified line 191, etcd line 287) run `doPlaylistTests`, which after creating playlists through the k8s client immediately queries the legacy endpoint `/api/playlists` and requires the same UIDs (line 523-531), and after each k8s update calls `getFromBothAPIs` comparing legacy DTO fields (line 547). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a detached goroutine with no synchronization, so these assertions race against the background write and the tests will be flaky – and given the cancelled-context problem in the goroutine they are likely to fail deterministically. The tests need to poll/retry the legacy endpoint, or mode 3 must flush legacy writes before responding.

Unit tests never verify (or wait for) the asynchronous legacy write

All mode-3 write tests (`Create`, `Delete`, `Update`, `DeleteCollection`) assert only on the value returned from unified storage and return immediately; nothing calls `m.AssertExpectations`/`AssertCalled` or waits for the goroutine that performs the legacy write. The central new behaviour of mode 3 – that legacy is also written – is therefore completely untested (the cancelled-context bug above would not be caught). Worse, the goroutine may invoke the shared `mock.Mock` after the sub-test has finished; if the arguments don't match a registered expectation testify panics from that goroutine and takes down the whole test binary. Add a synchronization point (e.g. a channel closed from the mock's Run function) and assert the legacy call happened with the expected arguments.

The added block duplicates the line `github.com/grafana/grafana/pkg/apimachinery v0.0.0-20240701135906-559738ce6ae1/go.mod h1:...` that already exists a few lines above, and inserts entries out of sorted order (grafana-azure-sdk-go after grafana/pkg/apimachinery). This indicates the file was hand-edited rather than regenerated with `go work sync`/`go mod tidy`; it is also unrelated to the dual-writer change and will churn/conflict with other PRs. Regenerate the file or drop these hunks from this PR.

`runSplitQuery` now maps every target through `datasource.applyTemplateVariables(query, request.scopedVars, request.filters)`, but the same method is still applied later by `DataSourceWithBackend.query()` for every target of the sub-request created in `runSplitGroupedQueries` (via `datasource.runQuery`). Since the limit is a licensing/abuse control, this is an enforcement hole. WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`) so the check and write are atomic.

rowsAffected == 0 wrongly reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached for existing devices on MySQL

`updateDevice` maps `rowsAffected == 0` to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. On MySQL, `RowsAffected()` reports *changed* rows, not matched rows (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set), so an UPDATE that matches an already-tracked device but writes identical column values (same client_ip/user_agent and an `updated_at` that truncates to the same second — MySQL DATETIME has second precision here) returns 0. In that case an existing, already-counted device is denied access with "device limit reached" even though it is within the limit. Additionally, this error value conflates two distinct conditions ("device not found/expired" vs "limit reached"), which makes the surfaced error misleading; the device-not-found case should be distinguished or detected via a SELECT/matched-rows check.

A referer containing `'` produces the literal `'` in the JS string (wrong targetOrigin), and a referer ending in a backslash escapes the closing quote, producing a JavaScript syntax error that kills the resize script. Use `escape_javascript` (`j`) and, better, pass only the scheme+host of the referer since postMessage expects an origin, not a full URL.

false_positives.candidate:
raw_html cook method stores and renders unsanitized remote HTML

`Post#cook` now returns `raw` verbatim when `cook_method == Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`, so posts created by `TopicEmbed.import` keep whatever HTML came from the remote source as their `cooked` value. The RSS path (`Jobs::PollFeed#poll_feed` -> `TopicEmbed.import(user, url, i.title, content)`) passes the feed body through with no tag/attribute whitelist at all (only `import_remote` filters tags via ruby-readability), and the resulting `cooked` is emitted with `<%= raw post.cooked %>` in app/views/embed/best.html.erb as well as in normal topic rendering. A hostile or compromised feed (or an XSS-laden page scraped from the embeddable host) can therefore inject `<script>`/`onerror` payloads that execute for every visitor of the forum. The imported HTML should be run through the existing sanitizer (e.g. Sanitize with a whitelist) before being stored as cooked.

`post.present?` does not detect a failed PostCreator run

`PostCreator#create` returns the (unsaved) Post object even when creation fails — it raises `ActiveRecord::Rollback` internally, which is swallowed, and the returned post has errors and a nil `id`/`topic_id`. `post.present?` is therefore true for failed creations, and the following `TopicEmbed.create!(topic_id: nil, post_id: nil, ...)` blows up with a NOT NULL/validation error, masking the real failure (e.g. a title that is too long or a rate limit). Check `post.persisted?` (or `post.errors.blank?`) instead, and bail out gracefully otherwise.

`open(url)` used without requiring 'open-uri'

`TopicEmbed.import_remote` calls `open(url).read` but topic_embed.rb only requires 'nokogiri'. `open-uri` is only required in app/jobs/scheduled/poll_feed.rb, which is not loaded on the `retrieve_topic` -> `TopicRetriever#fetch_http` path (that path only requires 'topic_retriever'/'topic_embed') unless feed polling happens to be enabled. Without open-uri loaded, `Kernel#open` treats the URL as a file name and raises `Errno::ENOENT`, so on-demand embed retrieval (and the disqus thor task) fails. Add `require 'open-uri'` to this file.

absolutize_urls corrupts protocol-relative URLs

The check `href.start_with?('/')` also matches protocol-relative URLs such as `//cdn.example.com/img.png`. After the substitution `src.sub(/^\/+/, '')` the result becomes `http://host/cdn.example.com/img.png`, i.e. a broken link/image for any feed that uses protocol-relative references (common for CDN-hosted assets). Protocol-relative URLs should be left alone or prefixed with the scheme only.

Existing embed with a deleted post raises NoMethodError

In the update branch `post = embed.post` can be nil (post hard-deleted, or a previous import that stored a bogus post_id). `PostRevisor.new(nil).revise!` then fails with a NoMethodError inside a Sidekiq job, and the embed row is never repaired. Guard for a missing post and either recreate the topic or skip.

Non-atomic SETNX + EXPIRE can permanently block retrieval of a URL

`$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` followed by a separate `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` is not atomic. If the process dies, the Redis connection fails, or the job is killed between the two calls, the key stays forever with no TTL, so `retrieved_recently?` returns true for that embed_url for the rest of the Redis instance's life and that page's discussion can never be retrieved (the embed iframe is stuck on the loading page). Use `$redis.set(key, "1", nx: true, ex: 60)` (or SETEX) instead.

Full feed poll executed inline during embed retrieval

`Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` runs the complete RSS/Atom poll synchronously (HTTP fetch of the feed plus creation/revision of a topic for every item) inside the `retrieve_topic` job each time an unknown embed_url is requested and feed polling is enabled. One cold embed view can therefore trigger a multi-second-to-minute import, and many concurrent unknown URLs will import the feed repeatedly in parallel (no locking), duplicating work and hammering the feed source. Enqueue the poll instead, or guard it with the same throttle used for HTTP retrieval.

`X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL` is not a valid header value

`ALLOWALL` is not a defined X-Frame-Options directive. Per the HTML spec/most current browsers an unrecognized value is treated as `DENY` (some older browsers ignored it), so setting this can actively prevent the page from being framed — exactly the opposite of the intent — and makes embedding fail on the browsers that follow the spec. To allow framing, delete the header that the default Rails/Discourse middleware set (`response.headers.delete('X-Frame-Options')`) and, if restriction is wanted, use a CSP `frame-ancestors` directive with the embeddable host.

`discourse_expires_in 1.minute` is applied to both branches, including the `render 'loading'` branch. The loading template reloads the iframe after 30s (app/views/embed/loading.html.erb), so the reload is served from the browser cache and shows the same "Loading Discussion..." page even after the topic has been retrieved; the user waits at least two cycles. Either skip caching (or use a much shorter max-age) when rendering the loading page, or make the reload cache-busting.

Spec stubs TopicView.new to return nil, so the rendered template raises

`TopicView.expects(:new).with(123, nil, {best: 5})` has no `returns`, so `@topic_view` is nil. The default `best` template then evaluates `@topic_view.posts.present?`, raising NoMethodError on nil during render, which makes the example (and the assertions in the `after` block) fail rather than verify the success path. The mock needs to return a double exposing `posts`/`topic`, or the spec should use `render_views false` with an explicit template stub.

Editing the existing CreateTopTopics migration to `create_table :top_topics, force: true` means that any environment which re-runs this migration (schema reload, `db:migrate:redo`, re-running from a reset schema_migrations) will silently `DROP TABLE top_topics` and all its rows instead of failing loudly. The same pattern is used in the new 20131217174004_create_topic_embeds migration. `force: true` has no benefit in a forward migration and should be removed.

The thread import was switched to `TopicEmbed.import_remote(user, t[:link], title: t[:title])`, which drops the previous `created_at: Date.parse(t[:created_at])`, so imported topics are now dated at import time instead of the original Disqus thread date, and the removed `--category` option means imported topics can no longer be placed in a category. If these behaviours are intentionally dropped, the option removal should at least be reflected in `TopicEmbed.import_remote` (accepting `created_at`/`category`) so existing import workflows are not silently degraded.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.

`self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={})` is defined at line 145 and then immediately redefined at line 149 as `self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={})`. In Ruby the second definition wins, so the width/height form is dead code and any existing caller doing `OptimizedImage.downsize(path, path, width, height)` now raises `ArgumentError: wrong number of arguments (4 for 2..3)`. The loop calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", ...)` with the same path as input and output and never inspects the return value. If `convert`/`ImageOptim` fails (which `convert_with` reports by returning false after swallowing the exception), the destination file — i.e. the user's original upload — may have already been truncated or left partially written, and the loop then runs up to 5 more times on the broken file before the (now corrupt) data is stored via `Upload.create_for`. The loop gives up after 5 iterations of 80% scaling. The new check uses `workingHours.find(workingHour => ... if (start < workingHour.startTime || end > workingHour.endTime) return true)` and then treats a match as "slot is outside of working hours" -> unavailable. Because `find` succeeds as soon as one range does not contain the slot, any schedule with more than one availability range applicable to the same weekday (split days such as 09:00-12:00 and 14:00-18:00, or ranges split across UTC midnight by `getWorkingHours`) will cause every slot to be rejected, producing an empty schedule. The predicate must instead require that *no* range contains the slot (e.g. `!workingHours.some(wh => wh.days.includes(day) && start >= wh.startTime && end <= wh.endTime)`).

Timezone-shifted date override wraps around midnight and silently loses availability

The override start/end are converted to minutes-of-day with `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, "minute").hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. When the invitee/organizer offset difference pushes the override across a day boundary (e.g. organizer 22:00-23:00 with a +8h invitee, or 02:00 with a -5h invitee), `hour()` wraps to the other day, so `startTime` can become greater than `endTime`. `buildSlots` then drops such a range via its `if (start >= end) continue` guard (or produces slots at completely wrong times), so the override silently yields no availability for invitees in far-away timezones.

Override offset depends on an optional `timeZone` that falls back to the server timezone

`dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` is used to compute the organizer offset, but `TimeRange.timeZone` is declared optional in `packages/types/schedule.d.ts`. If any caller of `getSlots` passes date overrides without `timeZone` (only the slots router was updated to attach it), `dayjs.tz(undefined)` resolves to the dayjs default/system timezone, producing a wrong organizer offset and silently shifted override slots instead of an error. Either make `timeZone` required for the overrides consumed here or explicitly fall back to the organizer timezone already passed into `getSlots`.

The PR's primary change is that fixed-host date overrides are honoured for ROUND_ROBIN events (via the new `dateOverrides`/`workingHours` arguments to `checkIfIsAvailable`), but no test creates a round-robin event with a fixed host that has a date override, so that code path is unverified. The added test only re-requests the same personal event with a different invitee timezone and asserts identical UTC slots; it does not exercise an organizer whose schedule timezone differs from the invitee's, and it does not cover a day that has both a date override and an existing booking (where the current implementation returns the slot as available).

One failing cancellation aborts the whole cancellation batch and leaves DB rows untouched forever

The whole `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop is wrapped in a single try/catch. If any single `client.request(...)` throws (invalid/expired batch id, SendGrid already has the batch in `cancel` status, transient 5xx), the loop is abandoned: all remaining reminders in the batch are never cancelled and their emails get sent. In addition, the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` objects are Prisma lazy promises that only execute when awaited in `Promise.all` at line 74; because the throw happens before that await, none of the already-processed reminders are deleted. On the next CRON run the same reminders are selected again, the same request fails again, and the cancellation pass is permanently stuck. Each reminder needs its own try/catch (and its delete should be awaited/committed per item).

remindersToCancel query is missing method/referenceId filters

`prisma.workflowReminder.findMany({ where: { cancelled: true, scheduledDate: { lte: ... } } })` does not filter on `method: WorkflowMethods.EMAIL` nor on `referenceId: { not: null }`, unlike every other query in this file. Any row that is flagged `cancelled` but has no `referenceId`, or that belongs to a non-email method, is posted to the SendGrid scheduled_sends endpoint with `batch_id: null`/a Twilio SID, which produces an error that (per the single try/catch above) aborts the whole cancellation pass. Restrict the query to email reminders with a non-null `referenceId`.

try/catch around the reminder cancellation cannot catch anything

The `try { originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach(...) } catch (error) { log.error(...) }` block wraps synchronous `forEach` calls over async functions. Since the returned promises are not awaited, any rejection from `deleteScheduledEmailReminder`/`deleteScheduledSMSReminder` escapes this catch as an unhandled rejection, and the log message is never produced. Await the calls (e.g. `await Promise.all(originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.map(...))`) so the error handling actually works and the cancellations complete before the reschedule continues.

Cancellation window can be too late for SendGrid's cancellation deadline

Cancellation is deferred to this CRON, which (per the PR description) runs every 15 minutes and only picks up reminders whose `scheduledDate` is within the next hour. SendGrid only honours a cancel request if it arrives sufficiently ahead of the send time (documented as at least 10 minutes). If a booking is cancelled shortly after a CRON run and its reminder is due in ~15–25 minutes, the next run can reach SendGrid with less than 10 minutes to spare and the cancellation is rejected, so the reminder for the cancelled booking is still delivered. Consider cancelling immediately (or on a much tighter schedule) for reminders due within the next hour, or widening/short-circuiting the window.

Type-only imports moved into a value import, and formatting will fail lint

`PrismaPromise` is a type-only export of `@prisma/client` but is now pulled in through a value import, and the import list `  Prisma\n} from "@prisma/client";` is missing the trailing comma required by the repo's prettier config, so `yarn lint`/format checks will fail on this file. Keep `import type { Prisma, PrismaPromise } from "@prisma/client";` for the type-only names and run prettier (the large commented-out `testAction` block was also re-indented by this change, adding unrelated diff noise).

Any downstream consumer of `user.organization` for dynamic bookings (e.g. building org-scoped booker URLs) will now see `undefined`, and the two branches of `loadUsers` return structurally different user shapes, which weakens the inferred type the comment claims to rely on. Re-add the select unless you have verified no consumer reads it.

Recurring cancellation now issues duplicated delete calls per calendar reference

The recurring branch (iterate all of the user's calendar credentials × all `updatedBookings`' first calendar reference) was moved inside the new `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)` loop. With N calendar references on a booking the whole credential×booking deletion matrix is executed N times, sending the same `deleteEvent` request repeatedly to each provider (and pushing N× duplicate promises into `apiDeletes`). For multi-host collective recurring events this multiplies external API calls and the risk of rate limiting. Hoist the recurring handling out of the per-reference loop.

Credential-less destinations create events in every credential of that integration

For each destination without a `credentialId`, the code creates an event in every calendar credential of the matching integration type (`this.calendarCredentials.filter((c) => c.type === destination.integration)`). Now that `destinationCalendar` is an array and is populated with each collective host's calendar, two hosts with credential-less Google destination calendars cause 2 × (number of google credentials) event creations, i.e. duplicate calendar entries for the same booking. Additionally the resulting `EventResult`s carry no `externalId`, so the persisted booking references lose the external calendar id. De-duplicate destinations and pass the destination's `externalId` through.

No tests for the array-based destinationCalendar behaviour

This PR changes `CalendarEvent.destinationCalendar` from a single object to an array across ~20 files and adds new branching in `createAllCalendarEvents`/`updateAllCalendarEvents` (per-destination credential resolution, DB credential fallback, collective host aggregation), yet no unit/integration tests were added and the only test touched is an e2e expectation value. Given the number of null/empty-array edge cases introduced (see the Google Meet crash and the dropped collective calendars), at least tests covering: empty destinationCalendar, destination without credentialId, and a collective event with two hosts, are needed before merge.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Module-level import promises can produce unhandled rejections and crash the process

Each `import("./x")` promise is created at module scope with no attached handler. If any single app module throws while being evaluated (bad/missing app key, failing SDK init, missing optional dependency), the resulting rejection is unhandled because nothing awaits that specific entry unless the app happens to be used. Under Node's default `--unhandled-rejections=throw` this terminates the process, so one broken app takes down the whole server even though no booking uses it. Previously a failing module was at least surfaced synchronously at import time of the specific consumer. Lazily created promises (thunks) or `.catch()` handling is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments address the same core concern: dynamic import failures are not handled gracefully and can crash the process. The candidate's suggestion of .catch() handling or lazy thunks is semantically equivalent to the golden comment's try-catch around the await.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
try/catch around forEach with async callback cannot catch failures anymore

Same problem as in the vital reschedule helper: the callback passed to `forEach` is now `async`, so the enclosing `try/catch` will never see errors thrown inside it; rejections from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent` or `deleteMeeting` become unhandled promise rejections rather than being logged, and the cancellations are not awaited before the function returns. Use a `for...of` loop with `await` inside the try block.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: an async callback passed to forEach is not awaited, so the surrounding try/catch cannot handle rejections and cleanup may be incomplete. The candidate's for...of recommendation is one of the golden comment's accepted fixes.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are started eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy

The object literal calls `import("./applecalendar")`, `import("./caldavcalendar")`, … at module evaluation time, which immediately kicks off loading of every app package the moment `@calcom/app-store` is imported. The promises are merely stored, so consumers `await` an already-running import. The net effect is that all ~28 app modules (and their transitive deps such as Stripe/Google/Exchange SDKs) are still evaluated on every request path that touches the app store — the stated goal of async/lazy loading is not achieved, and webpack will still fetch every generated chunk. To get real laziness the entries must be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with call sites invoking the thunk.

getCalendarCredentials now returns a Promise in its `calendar` field, changing its public contract

`getCalendarCredentials` still looks synchronous, but `calendar: getCalendar(credential)` is now a `Promise<Calendar | null>` instead of `Calendar | null`. Only `getConnectedCalendars` in this file was updated to `await item.calendar`; any other consumer of `getCalendarCredentials` (it is exported and used outside this module, e.g. destination-calendar/connected-calendar flows and the API app) that calls `item.calendar.listCalendars()` or checks `if (!item.calendar)` will now silently see a truthy Promise and break at runtime. Additionally, promises stored on entries that a caller never awaits can reject unobserved. The function should either be made `async` and resolve the calendars with `Promise.all`, or keep the credential list free of promises.

try/catch around forEach with async callback cannot catch failures anymore

Changing the callback to `async` means the surrounding `try { ... } catch { logger.error(...) }` block can never observe an error: the callback returns a promise that is discarded, so any rejection from `getCalendar` or `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` escapes as an unhandled promise rejection (process-level crash on modern Node) instead of being logged. The deletions are also not awaited before the reschedule email is sent. Replace with a `for...of` loop using `await` inside the try block.

Recurring-booking calendar deletions are pushed to apiDeletes after it is already awaited

In the recurring branch the credentials are still iterated with `.forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... apiDeletes.push(deletedEvent) })`. Because the callback is async, `apiDeletes.push` runs only after the awaits resolve — long after `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` at the end of the handler has captured the (still empty) array. So for "cancel all remaining recurring bookings" the external calendar deletions are neither awaited nor error-checked, and failures surface as unhandled rejections. The sibling non-credentialId branch in the same block was correctly converted to a `for...of` loop; this branch should be too.

Commented-out example entry points at a non-existent directory

The placeholder comment was changed from `// import * as example from "./_example";` to `// example: import("./example"),`. The directory in the repo is `_example`, so a developer who uncomments this line to register a new app gets a module-not-found error. It should read `// example: import("./_example"),`.
